32.plain: It is a federal crime to deliberately damage, destroy, or disable an aircraft covered by U.S. law, or to plant a bomb or dangerous substance on or near one. It is also a crime to damage air navigation equipment, attack people on board, interfere with flight crews, or knowingly give false information that puts a plane in flight at risk. Similar attacks on foreign-registered civil aircraft are covered too, as are threats to commit these acts.
keyPoints: Must be done willfully (on purpose)
Attempts and conspiracies (plans with others) are punished the same as completed acts
Foreign aircraft covered if a U.S. national was or would have been aboard, an offender is a U.S. national, or the offender is later found here
Serious threats to commit these acts are a separate, lesser crime
32.penalty: Up to 20 years in prison, a fine, or both; up to 5 years, a fine, or both for threats

33.plain: It is a federal crime to deliberately damage, tamper with, or plant explosives on or near a motor vehicle used in interstate or foreign commerce (such as a truck or bus crossing state lines), or its cargo. It also covers attacks on garages, terminals, and other facilities that support these vehicles, and disabling or harming drivers or workers. The act must be meant to endanger people or show reckless disregard for human life.
keyPoints: Must be willful, with intent to endanger people or reckless disregard for human life
Attempts and conspiracies are also crimes
Much harsher punishment if the vehicle was carrying high-level radioactive waste or spent nuclear fuel
33.penalty: Up to 20 years in prison, a fine, or both; at least 30 years up to life plus a fine if the vehicle carried high-level radioactive waste or spent nuclear fuel

35.plain: It is illegal to knowingly spread false information about an attempt (real or claimed) to commit certain crimes, such as attacks on aircraft, vehicles, trains, or ships covered by related chapters of federal law. Doing so knowingly can lead to a civil fine (a money penalty, not a criminal charge). Doing it willfully and maliciously, or with reckless disregard for human life, is a federal crime.
keyPoints: The person must know the information is false
Basic violation: civil penalty up to $1,000 collected through a lawsuit by the U.S.
Criminal charge requires malice or reckless disregard for human life
Covers hoaxes about crimes in this chapter and chapters 97 and 111
35.penalty: Civil penalty up to $1,000; if done willfully and maliciously or recklessly, up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both

36.plain: It is a federal crime to fire a weapon into a group of two or more people to intimidate, harass, injure, or maim them, when this is done to further or hide a major drug offense. A "major drug offense" means large-scale drug trafficking, drug conspiracies, or running a continuing drug enterprise as defined in federal drug laws. The punishment depends on whether someone is killed.
keyPoints: Must be connected to a major drug offense
Must intend to intimidate, harass, injure, or maim
Shooting must create grave risk to human life
Killing someone can bring any prison term up to life, or the death penalty for first-degree murder
36.penalty: Up to 25 years in prison and/or a fine; any term up to life if someone is killed, and death is possible for first-degree murder

37.plain: It is a federal crime to intentionally use a device, substance, or weapon to commit violence against a person at an airport serving international flights, if the act causes or is likely to cause serious injury or death. It is also a crime to destroy or seriously damage such an airport's facilities or parked civil aircraft, or to disrupt airport services, when this endangers safety at the airport.
keyPoints: Must be unlawful and intentional, using a device, substance, or weapon
Attempts and conspiracies are also covered
Applies abroad if the offender is later found in the U.S. or an offender or victim is a U.S. national
Conduct in the U.S. tied to a labor dispute that is a state felony cannot be prosecuted under this section
37.penalty: Up to 20 years in prison, a fine, or both; death or any term up to life if someone dies

38.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly commit fraud involving aircraft or space vehicle parts in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce. This includes lying about or hiding important facts about a part, using fake records, certificates, or labels, and selling, importing, exporting, or installing parts using fraudulent paperwork. Penalties grow if a faulty part causes serious injury or death.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly and with intent to defraud (deceive for gain)
Attempts and conspiracies are also crimes
Organizations face fines up to $10 million or $20 million
Courts must order forfeiture (government seizure) of proceeds and may seize property used in the crime
38.penalty: In general, up to 10 years, a fine, or both; up to 15 years and/or $500,000 if a part with faked quality is installed; up to 20 years and/or $1,000,000 if it causes serious injury; any term up to life and/or $1,000,000 if it causes a death

39.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly sell a traffic signal preemption transmitter (a device that can change a traffic light's timing or sequence) to someone not authorized to use one. It is also a crime for an unauthorized person to use one. Authorized users include people acting for agencies or companies that provide services like fire, police, ambulance, transit, or maintenance for a government.
keyPoints: Selling must be done knowingly
Use for classroom or instructional purposes is not covered
Applies to conduct in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce
39.penalty: Selling: up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both; unauthorized use: up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both

39A.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly aim a laser pointer at an aircraft, or at its flight path, when the aircraft is under U.S. jurisdiction. This applies to anyone, with limited exceptions.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Exceptions for authorized aircraft research and flight testing
Exceptions for Defense and Homeland Security work and for laser emergency distress signals
The Attorney General may create more exceptions by regulation

39B.plain: It is a federal crime to fly a drone (unmanned aircraft) in a way that knowingly or recklessly interferes with an aircraft carrying people, creating an immediate safety hazard. It is also a crime to knowingly fly a drone without authorization in a "runway exclusion zone" (an area around active runways at certain controlled airports, extending 1 mile past each runway end and half a mile wide).
keyPoints: Interference can be knowing or reckless (ignoring an obvious risk)
Runway zone offense requires knowing, unauthorized flight
Penalties increase sharply if serious injury or death results
39B.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both; up to 10 years if reckless interference causes serious injury or death; any term up to life if knowing interference or a runway-zone violation causes (or attempts or conspires to cause) serious injury or death

40.plain: Drivers of commercial motor vehicles (such as large trucks) must stop for inspection when directed by an authorized Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration employee at or near an inspection site, and must not leave until allowed. It is a federal crime to knowingly fail to stop or to leave without permission.
keyPoints: Applies only to commercial motor vehicle drivers
Inspection can cover the vehicle, driver, cargo, and required records
Must be done knowingly
40.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both

40A.plain: It is a federal crime to fly a drone (unmanned aircraft) in a way that knowingly or recklessly interferes with efforts to fight a wildfire, or with related law enforcement or emergency response.

Does not apply to government drone operations (or their contractors) for public safety, firefighting, law enforcement, or emergency response

41.plain: It is a federal crime to hunt, trap, capture, willfully disturb, or kill any bird, fish, or wild animal on federal lands or waters set aside as wildlife sanctuaries, refuges, or breeding grounds, unless allowed by official rules. Taking or destroying eggs or nests there is also covered, as is willfully damaging U.S. government property on those lands.
keyPoints: Activities allowed by lawful rules and regulations are not crimes
Disturbing wildlife or damaging property must be willful (on purpose)
Applies only on federally reserved refuge or sanctuary lands and waters
41.penalty: Up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both

42.plain: It is a federal crime to bring into the U.S. (or ship between U.S. states and territories) certain harmful animal species, such as mongooses, flying foxes, zebra and quagga mussels, bighead carp, brown tree snakes, and others the Interior Secretary lists as dangerous to people, farming, forests, or wildlife. It is also illegal to knowingly cause wild animals or birds to be shipped into the U.S. under inhumane or unhealthy conditions.
keyPoints: Prohibited animals must be exported or destroyed at the importer's expense
Permits may allow imports for zoos, education, medicine, or science
Dead museum specimens, canaries, parrots, and certain cage birds are allowed
Many dead, sick, or starving animals on arrival is strong evidence of inhumane shipping
42.penalty: Up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both

43.plain: It is a federal crime to travel across state lines or use the mail or other interstate means to damage or interfere with an animal enterprise (such as a farm, lab, zoo, pet store, rodeo, or animal shelter), when this involves intentionally damaging property or putting someone in reasonable fear of death or serious injury through threats, vandalism, harassment, or intimidation. People and businesses connected to the enterprise are also protected.
keyPoints: Must intend to damage or interfere with an animal enterprise's operations
Attempts and conspiracies are also crimes
Penalty depends on economic damage and injuries caused
Peaceful protest and lawful boycotts protected by the First Amendment are not covered
43.penalty: A fine, up to 1 year in prison, or both for little or no harm; up to 5, 10, or 20 years (and/or a fine) as damage, fear, or injury increase; any term up to life if someone dies

47.plain: It is a federal crime to use an aircraft or motor vehicle to hunt wild, unbranded horses or burros on public lands in order to capture or kill them. It is also a crime to pollute a watering hole on public lands to trap, kill, or injure these animals.
keyPoints: Protects wild unbranded horses, mares, colts, and burros on public land or ranges
Hunting must be for capturing or killing
"Aircraft" and "motor vehicle" are defined broadly

48.plain: It is a federal crime to purposely crush, burn, drown, suffocate, impale, or otherwise seriously injure a living animal (mammal, bird, reptile, or amphibian) when connected to interstate commerce or federal land. It is also a crime to knowingly create, sell, or share obscene "animal crush videos" showing this, including some made abroad and brought into the U.S.
keyPoints: Crushing must be purposeful; creating or distributing videos must be knowing
Exceptions: normal veterinary and farm practices, food slaughter, hunting and fishing, research, protecting people or property, humane euthanasia
Good-faith sharing of videos with law enforcement is allowed
Accidental conduct that hurts an animal is not covered
48.penalty: Up to 7 years in prison, a fine, or both

81.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully and maliciously set fire to or burn any building, structure, vessel, machinery, supplies, military stores, or navigation aids within special federal jurisdiction (such as federal lands, military bases, or U.S. ships at sea). Attempts and conspiracies are also covered.
keyPoints: Must be willful and malicious (intentional and wrongful)
Fine can equal the cost of repairing or replacing damaged property
Burning a home or endangering someone's life brings up to life in prison

111.plain: It is a federal crime to forcibly assault, resist, oppose, impede, intimidate, or interfere with a federal officer or employee covered by section 1114 while they are on duty or because of their work. It is also a crime to forcibly assault or intimidate a former federal officer or employee because of their past official duties.
keyPoints: Conduct must be forcible
Physical contact or intent to commit another felony raises the penalty
Using a deadly or dangerous weapon or causing injury brings the highest penalty
Applies even to conduct outside the U.S.
111.penalty: Up to 1 year, a fine, or both for simple assault; up to 8 years with physical contact or intent to commit another felony; up to 20 years with a weapon or bodily injury

112.plain: It is a federal crime to assault, strike, wound, imprison, or attack a foreign official, official guest, or internationally protected person (such as a diplomat), or to violently attack their office, home, or vehicle in a way likely to endanger them. Attempts are also covered. It is also a crime to willfully intimidate, threaten, harass, or obstruct a foreign official or guest, or to gather with two or more others near a foreign mission intending to break this law.
keyPoints: Using a deadly weapon or causing injury raises the penalty
Harassment, intimidation, and gatherings near missions must be willful
Activity protected by the First Amendment is not restricted
Some attacks abroad can be prosecuted in the U.S.
112.penalty: Up to 3 years, a fine, or both for assault; up to 10 years with a weapon or bodily injury; up to 6 months for intimidation, harassment, or unlawful gatherings

113.plain: It is a federal crime to commit an assault within special federal jurisdiction (such as federal lands, military bases, or U.S. ships). The punishment depends on the type of assault, from simple assault to assault with intent to murder.

Higher penalties when the victim is under 16 or a spouse, intimate, or dating partner

114.plain: It is a federal crime, within special federal jurisdiction (such as federal lands or U.S. ships), to cut, bite, disable, or destroy another person's nose, ear, lip, tongue, eye, limb, or other body part with intent to torture, maim, or disfigure them. Throwing or pouring scalding water, acid, or caustic substances on someone with the same intent is also covered.
keyPoints: Must intend to torture, maim (permanently injure), or disfigure
Covers acid or scalding-liquid attacks

115.plain: It is a federal crime to assault, kidnap, murder, or threaten a family member of a U.S. official, federal judge, or federal law enforcement officer, or to threaten those officials themselves, in order to interfere with or get revenge for their official work. It also protects former officials and their families from retaliation for past duties.

Attempts and conspiracies to kidnap or murder are covered
Kidnapping and murder penalties are set by other sections (1201, 1111, 1113, 1117)
Applies to conduct outside the U.S.

116.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly perform, attempt, or conspire to perform female genital mutilation (non-medical cutting or injury of external female genitals) on anyone under 18. Parents, guardians, or caretakers who allow or arrange it, and anyone who transports a minor for this purpose, can also be charged. There must be a link to interstate or foreign commerce or federal territory.
keyPoints: Victim must be under 18
Must be done knowingly
Medically necessary surgery by licensed practitioners, including during childbirth, is allowed
Religion, custom, or tradition is not a defense

117.plain: It is a federal crime to commit a domestic assault (an assault on a current or former spouse, partner, child, parent, or similar family or household member) within special federal jurisdiction or Indian country, if the person already has at least 2 prior convictions for domestic violence-type offenses or stalking and protection-order offenses.

Causing substantial bodily injury raises the maximum penalty

118.plain: It is a federal crime to block, resist, or interfere with a federal law enforcement agent who is carrying out certain protective duties. These are protection duties authorized under State Department and Diplomatic Security laws, such as guarding officials or foreign dignitaries. The law covers conduct inside the United States or in U.S. maritime areas under federal control.

Applies only when the agent is performing specific protective duties
Covers obstructing, resisting, or interfering, not just physical attacks

119.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly post or share certain private information about a protected person or their close family so the public can see it, when meant to threaten, intimidate, or encourage violence against them. Protected people include federal officers and employees, jurors, court officers, witnesses, informants, and state or local officers who help federal investigations. Private information includes Social Security numbers, home addresses, personal phone numbers, and personal email.

Protects the covered person's immediate family too
Covered information: SSN, home address, home/mobile phone, personal email, home fax

152.plain: It is a federal crime to cheat or lie in a bankruptcy case. This includes hiding property from the court or creditors, making false sworn statements or claims, fraudulently receiving a debtor's property after a case is filed, giving or taking bribes connected to the case, and hiding, destroying, faking, or withholding financial records. It applies to debtors, creditors, and anyone else involved in the case.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly and fraudulently
Covers hiding or transferring property in expectation of a bankruptcy or to defeat bankruptcy law
Includes giving or taking payment to act or not act in a bankruptcy case

153.plain: It is a federal crime for people who help run a bankruptcy estate (the debtor's property managed by the court) to steal or misuse its property or to hide or destroy its documents. 154.plain: It is a federal crime for a bankruptcy trustee, custodian, marshal, or other court officer to buy property from an estate they are in charge of. 155.plain: It is a federal crime for people involved in a bankruptcy or receivership case (such as debtors, creditors, trustees, receivers, or their attorneys) to knowingly and fraudulently agree with each other to fix the fees paid out of the estate. The agreement can be spoken, written, or implied

156.plain: It is a federal crime for a bankruptcy petition preparer (a paid non-lawyer who prepares bankruptcy filings) to knowingly ignore bankruptcy law or court rules if that causes the case to be dismissed. The debtor's own attorney and the attorney's employees are not petition preparers.

157.plain: It is a federal crime to use the bankruptcy system as part of a scheme to cheat people. 175.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly develop, make, stockpile, transfer, obtain, keep, or possess any biological agent, toxin, or delivery system for use as a weapon, or to help a foreign country or group do so. Attempts, threats, and conspiracies (agreements to commit the crime) are also crimes. 175b.plain: It is a federal crime for certain restricted people to ship, transport, possess, or receive dangerous listed germs or toxins (called select agents) when this involves interstate or foreign commerce. Restricted people include those charged with or convicted of serious crimes, fugitives, illegal drug users, people in the U.S. unlawfully, and members of terrorist groups, among others. 175c.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly make, engineer, obtain, transfer, receive, possess, import, export, or use variola virus (the virus that causes smallpox), or to possess it and threaten to use it. Attempts and conspiracies are also covered. It applies to conduct affecting U.S. commerce, conduct by or against U.S. nationals abroad, and conduct against U.S. government property.

201.plain: It is a federal crime to bribe a federal public official, or for an official to demand or accept a bribe, to influence an official act or get them to break their duty or allow fraud on the United States. It is also a crime to corruptly give, offer, or promise—or to demand or accept—anything of value to influence a witness's sworn testimony or to keep a witness away. A lesser offense covers illegal gratuities (gifts given or taken because of an official act or testimony), even without a corrupt deal.

203.plain: It is a federal crime for members of Congress, federal officers, employees, and judges (and D.C. employees) to ask for or accept pay for representing others before the government in matters where the government is a party or has a direct and substantial interest. It is also a crime to knowingly offer or give them such pay. This section does not set its own penalty; the punishment is set in section 216.

Special Government employees (temporary or part-time) are covered only for certain matters

204.plain: It is a federal crime for a member of Congress or member-elect to practice law in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims or the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. This section does not set its own penalty; punishment is set in section 216.

207.plain: This law limits lobbying and representation by former federal officials after they leave government (often called the "revolving door" law). Former executive branch employees may never represent others to the government on specific matters they personally worked on, and face 1- or 2-year bans on other contacts depending on their role and seniority. Former members of Congress and senior congressional staff face 1- or 2-year bans on lobbying Congress, senior officials face a 1-year ban on representing or advising foreign governments or parties, and former trade or treaty negotiators and private-sector workers loaned to an agency face 1-year limits on helping others with those talks or that agency's contracts. This section does not set its own penalty; punishment is set in section 216.

Senators face a 2-year ban; House members and senior staff face 1 year

209.plain: It is a federal crime for an executive branch or D.C. employee to receive salary or salary supplements for their government work from anyone other than the U.S. government. It is also a crime for any person or organization to pay such a supplement. Payments from a state, county, or city treasury are allowed. 219.plain: It is a federal crime for a public official to work as an agent of a foreign government or other foreign principal when that role requires registration under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. 220.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly and willfully pay, offer, ask for, or accept kickbacks, bribes, or other payments for referring patients to addiction recovery homes, substance use treatment facilities, or laboratories. 228.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully fail to pay child support for a child living in another state when the debt is more than 1 year overdue or more than $5,000. 231.plain: It is a federal crime to teach or demonstrate how to make or use firearms, explosives, firebombs, or harmful techniques, knowing or intending they will be used unlawfully in a civil disorder (a violent public disturbance, such as a riot). 241.plain: It is a federal crime for two or more people to conspire (agree together) to injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate anyone in using a right protected by the U.S. Constitution or federal law, or to punish them for having used it. It is also a crime for two or more people to go in disguise on a highway or someone's property to stop a person from exercising such rights.
keyPoints: Requires at least two people acting together
Protects anyone exercising constitutional or federal legal rights
Harsher penalties if death results or the acts include kidnapping, aggravated sexual abuse, or attempted murder
241.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both; up to life in prison or death if someone dies or the acts include kidnapping, aggravated sexual abuse, or attempted murder

242.plain: It is a federal crime for someone acting under color of law (using power given by a government role, such as a police officer or official) to willfully deprive a person of rights protected by the Constitution or federal law. It is also a crime to give someone different punishments because they are a noncitizen or because of their race or color.
keyPoints: Must be done willfully
Applies to people acting with government authority
Higher penalty if bodily injury results or a dangerous weapon, explosives, or fire is used
Highest penalty if death results or acts include kidnapping, aggravated sexual abuse, or attempted murder
242.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both; up to 10 years if bodily injury results or a weapon, explosives, or fire is used; up to life or death if someone dies or for kidnapping, aggravated sexual abuse, or attempted murder

243.plain: It is a federal crime for an official responsible for selecting or summoning jurors to exclude or fail to summon a qualified citizen because of race, color, or past status as a slave. This applies to juries in both federal and state courts, including grand juries and trial juries.

Protects citizens who are otherwise qualified to serve
Covers both federal and state courts
243.penalty: A fine of up to $5,000; no prison term

act: exclude or fail to summon a qualified citizen because of race, color, or past status as a slave

244.plain: It is a federal crime for an owner, manager, or employee of a theater or other public entertainment place to cause someone to be discriminated against because they are wearing a U.S. military uniform. It applies only in the District of Columbia and U.S. territories and possessions.
keyPoints: Applies to owners, managers, and employees of entertainment venues
Protects people wearing any U.S. armed forces uniform
Limited to D.C. and U.S. territories and possessions

245.plain: It is a federal crime to use force or threats of force to willfully injure, intimidate, or interfere with someone because they are voting, using federal programs, serving on a jury, or taking part in other protected activities. It also covers interfering with someone because of race, color, religion, or national origin while they attend public school, work, travel, or use public places like hotels and restaurants. It applies whether or not the offender is acting with government authority.
keyPoints: Must be willful and involve force or threat of force
Federal prosecution requires written approval from top Justice Department officials
Small owner-occupied lodging with 5 or fewer rental rooms is exempt for some provisions
Penalties rise with bodily injury, weapons, fire, death, kidnapping, or sexual abuse
245.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both; up to 10 years if bodily injury results or a weapon, explosives, or fire is used; up to life or death if someone dies or for kidnapping, aggravated sexual abuse, or attempted murder

246.plain: It is a federal crime to take away, try to take away, or threaten to take away a person's job, pay, or other benefit funded by federal relief or work-relief money because of their political affiliation, race, color, sex, religion, or national origin.
keyPoints: Covers benefits paid for wholly or partly by federal relief funding
Includes direct, indirect, attempted, and threatened actions
Protects against bias based on politics, race, color, sex, religion, or national origin
246.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: deprives, attempts to deprive, or threatens to deprive any person of any employment, position, work, compensation, or other benefit

act: take away, try to take away, or threaten to take away a person's job, pay, or other benefit

247.plain: It is a federal crime to intentionally deface, damage, or destroy religious property (such as a church, synagogue, mosque, or religious cemetery) because of its religious character, or to use force or threats to stop someone from practicing their religion, when the act affects interstate or foreign commerce. It is also a crime to damage religious property because of the race, color, or ethnicity of people connected with it. Attempts are covered too.
keyPoints: Must be intentional
Federal prosecution requires written approval from the Attorney General or a designee
Penalties increase with property damage over $5,000, injury, fire or explosives, or death
Non-capital charges must be filed within 7 years
247.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison and a fine; up to 3 years if damage exceeds $5,000; up to 20 years if injury results or a weapon, explosives, or fire is used; up to 40 years if injury results from fire or explosives; up to life or death if someone dies or for kidnapping, aggravated sexual abuse, or attempted murder

248.plain: It is a federal crime to use force, threats of force, or physical obstruction to intentionally injure, intimidate, or interfere with someone getting or providing reproductive health services, or someone practicing religion at a place of worship. It is also a crime to intentionally damage a reproductive health facility because of its services, or to damage a place of religious worship. Victims and government attorneys can also sue for money damages and court orders.
keyPoints: Must be intentional; peaceful picketing and other First Amendment protected expression are not covered
Parents or guardians are not liable for acts directed only at their own minor child
Nonviolent blocking of entrances carries lower penalties
Civil lawsuits can seek $5,000 per violation or civil penalties up to $25,000
248.penalty: First offense: up to 1 year and a fine; repeat: up to 3 years. Nonviolent obstruction: up to 6 months and $10,000 (first), 18 months and $25,000 (repeat). Up to 10 years if injury results; up to life if death results

249.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully cause bodily injury to someone, or attempt to do so with fire, a gun, a dangerous weapon, or explosives, because of the person's actual or perceived race, color, religion, or national origin. It is also a crime when the attack is because of gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, or disability, if it involves interstate travel or commerce or happens on federal land. Conspiracies that result in death or serious injury are also punished.
keyPoints: Must be willful and motivated by the victim's actual or perceived identity
Bodily injury does not include purely emotional or psychological harm
Federal prosecution requires written certification from the Attorney General or a designee
7-year time limit to charge, except no limit when death results
249.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both; up to life if someone dies or the crime includes kidnapping, aggravated sexual abuse, or attempted murder; conspiracies causing death or serious injury: up to 30 years

285.plain: It is a federal crime to take, without permission, any document filed or kept by the U.S. government that is meant to be used to get money from the government or support a claim against it. It is also a crime to use or try to use such a taken document to get payment from the government.

Covers records like affidavits, receipts, vouchers, and powers of attorney
Applies whether or not the claim was already used or paid

286.plain: It is a federal crime to agree or conspire with others to cheat the U.S. government or any federal agency by getting, or helping someone get, payment of a false or fraudulent claim.

Covers claims to any federal department, agency, or official
Includes military and civilian government claims

289.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly and willfully submit false or fraudulent documents about a pension claim or any other matter handled by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs. 290.plain: It is a federal crime for a claim agent, attorney, or other person collecting pay or pension claims for a service member or veteran to keep that person's military discharge papers without the owner's consent, or to refuse to return them when asked. 291.plain: It is a federal crime for a federal judge, court clerk, U.S. attorney, marshal, magistrate judge, or other federal official to buy, for less than full value, a claim against the U.S. for the fees, mileage, or expenses owed to a witness, juror, or court officer. 331.plain: It is a federal crime to fraudulently alter, damage, shave down, or lighten U.S. coins, or foreign coins that are legal or in use as money in the United States. It is also a crime to fraudulently possess, pass, sell, or bring into the country such coins while knowing they have been altered.

332.plain: It is a federal crime for an officer or worker at a U.S. mint or assay office (a government office that tests metal purity) to debase gold or silver coins by lowering their gold or silver content or weight, or to fraudulently tamper with the mint's scales or weights. Covers embezzling metals, coins, medals, or other money in their charge

334.plain: It is a federal crime for a Federal Reserve Agent, their staff, or an employee of the Federal Reserve Board to issue or circulate Federal Reserve notes in violation of the laws governing how those notes are issued. 351.plain: It is a federal crime to kill, kidnap, attempt to kill or kidnap, conspire to kill or kidnap, or assault certain top federal officials. Protected people include Members of Congress (and those elected), Cabinet department heads and their second-in-command, top intelligence and CIA leaders, major presidential and vice presidential candidates, and Supreme Court Justices, plus nominees for some of these posts. 17.plain: This section sets the federal insanity defense. A defendant is not guilty if a severe mental illness or defect made them unable to understand the nature or wrongfulness of their acts, and the defendant must prove this by clear and convincing evidence.

25.plain: This section raises the punishment for adults (18 or older) who use a minor to commit a federal violent crime or to help avoid getting caught. The maximum prison time and fine for the underlying crime double for a first conviction and triple for later convictions.

26.plain: This section defines "seaport" for federal criminal law: piers, wharves, docks, and similar structures where ships can tie up, plus the nearby land, water, buildings, and equipment.

34.plain: This section adds punishment for crimes in the aircraft and motor vehicle chapter that cause someone's death. In those cases the offender can face the death penalty or life in prison.

158.plain: This section requires the Attorney General to assign federal prosecutors and FBI agents in each district to focus on bankruptcy crimes involving abusive debt agreements and seriously false bankruptcy papers. Bankruptcy courts must set up ways to refer such cases to them.

175a.plain: This section lets the Attorney General ask the Secretary of Defense for military help in enforcing the federal ban on biological weapons during an emergency involving a biological weapon of mass destruction.

176.plain: This section lets the government seize, take ownership of (forfeit), and destroy biological agents, toxins, or delivery systems tied to biological weapons crimes or with no apparent peaceful purpose. Owners get notice and a hearing, and can defend by showing a reasonable peaceful purpose.

177.plain: This section lets the United States go to civil court to get an order (an injunction) stopping biological weapons activity, or work with dangerous biological agents that has no apparent peaceful purpose. Showing a reasonable peaceful purpose is a defense.

206.plain: This section says certain conflict-of-interest rules (sections 203 and 205) do not apply to retired military and uniformed-service officers who are not on active duty and do not otherwise work for the government.

216.plain: This section sets the punishments for several federal conflict-of-interest crimes (sections 203, 204, 205, 207, 208, and 209): up to 1 year in prison, or up to 5 years if done willfully, plus fines. It also allows civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation (or more) and court orders to stop the conduct.

218.plain: This section lets the President or agency heads cancel contracts, licenses, grants, and other government benefits connected to a conviction under the bribery and conflict-of-interest chapter. The government can also recover what it paid or gave.

229A.plain: This section sets the punishments for chemical weapons crimes under section 229: a fine and prison for any number of years, or death or life in prison if someone is killed. It also allows civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation and requires convicted people to repay cleanup and storage costs.

229B.plain: This section requires people convicted of chemical weapons crimes to give up (forfeit) property used in or gained from the crime, and sets the procedures for seizing it. It also covers destroying seized chemical weapons and makes owners pay the related costs.

229C.plain: This section makes clear that the chemical weapons laws do not ban personal self-defense devices such as pepper spray or mace.

229D.plain: This section lets the United States go to civil court to get an order (an injunction) stopping prohibited chemical weapons activity or preparations for it.

229E.plain: This section lets the Attorney General ask the Secretary of Defense for military help in enforcing the chemical weapons ban during an emergency involving a chemical weapon.

233.plain: This section says the federal civil disorder laws do not replace state or local laws on the same subject. State laws stay valid unless they conflict with the purposes of this chapter.

497.plain: It is a federal crime to forge or alter letters patent (official land or rights grants) issued by the President, or to knowingly pass such forged papers as real.

Attempts to pass are covered

pass such forged papers as real

498.plain: It is a federal crime to forge or falsely alter a military or naval discharge certificate, or to knowingly use, possess, or show a fake one.
keyPoints: Using or possessing requires knowing it is fake
498.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both

use, possess, or show a fake one

499.plain: It is a federal crime to forge or tamper with official U.S. military or government passes or permits, use them to defraud, pretend to be the person a pass was issued to, or willfully let someone else use your pass.

Lending your pass to others must be willful

500.plain: It is a federal crime to forge, alter, or fraudulently issue or cash postal money orders, or to steal or knowingly receive blank money order forms. It also covers stealing or misusing money order machines and stamping tools.

Receiving stolen blank forms requires knowing they were stolen
Covers foreign postal money orders payable in the U.S.

501.plain: It is a federal crime to forge postage stamps, meter stamps, stamped envelopes, or postal cards, or to knowingly use, sell, or possess fakes to use or sell. It is also a crime to print official postage without Postal Service authority.
keyPoints: Using, selling, or possessing fakes must be knowing
Unauthorized printing of real-style postage is covered
Delivering printed stamps to unauthorized people requires intent to defraud

502.plain: It is a federal crime to forge a foreign government's postage or revenue stamps, or to knowingly use or pass forged ones.
keyPoints: Using forged stamps must be knowing
Covers foreign postage and revenue (tax) stamps
502.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: forges, or counterfeits, or knowingly utters or uses any forged or counterfeit postage stamp or revenue stamp of any foreign government

use or pass forged ones

503.plain: It is a federal crime to forge postmarking stamps or postmarks to make them look genuine, or to make, knowingly use, sell, or possess to use or sell any forged postmarking stamp or tool.
keyPoints: Forging an impression requires intent to make it look genuine
Use, sale, or possession must be knowing
503.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both

504.plain: This section lists when it is legal to print, film, or import pictures of U.S. and foreign stamps, money, and securities. It sets rules on color, size, and destroying the printing plates, and lets the Treasury Secretary allow some color and electronic copies.

505.plain: It is a federal crime to forge the signature of a federal judge or other court officer, or to fake the seal of a federal court, to make a court document look real. It is also a crime to knowingly use or hand in as evidence a document with a fake signature or seal.
keyPoints: Applies to courts of the United States and its Territories
Using or submitting a fake requires knowing it is fake
Purpose is to make a proceeding or document look authentic
505.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both

506.plain: It is a federal crime to fake, forge, or alter the official seal of any U.S. government department or agency. It is also a crime to knowingly put a fake seal on a document, or to sell, own, ship, or import a fake seal with intent to cheat (fraudulent intent).
keyPoints: Using a fake seal must be done knowingly
Selling, owning, or shipping a fake seal requires fraudulent intent
Each fake seal is a separate offense
Tougher penalties if done to help a non-citizen get federal benefits they are not entitled to

507.plain: It is a federal crime to fake or alter official papers for ships, such as ownership certificates, clearance papers, or customs documents. It is also a crime to pass off such fake papers as real, knowing they are fake, with intent to cheat.
keyPoints: Covers ship documents issued under U.S. authority and customs papers
Passing fake papers requires knowing they are fake
Passing fake papers requires intent to defraud
507.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison, a fine, or both

utters, publishes, or passes, or attempts to utter, publish, or pass, as true, any such false, forged, counterfeited, or falsely altered instrument

508.plain: It is a federal crime to fake or knowingly alter the government forms used to request travel from carriers (like airlines or railroads) on the government's account. It is also a crime to knowingly use, sell, or try to pass off such fake or altered forms.
keyPoints: Altering a real form must be done knowingly
Passing or selling fake forms must be done knowingly
Attempts are also covered
508.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both

509.plain: It is a federal crime to make, own, or use plates or other tools for printing government travel request forms without permission. It is also a crime to make or sell copies of those forms or bring such plates or copies into the United States.
keyPoints: Owning or using printing plates is a crime unless done with lawful authority
Covers making look-alike plates and copies of the forms
Bringing such items into the U.S. is also covered

510.plain: It is a federal crime to forge a signature or endorsement (the signature on the back) on a U.S. Treasury check, bond, or security with intent to cheat, or to cash or pass one that has a forged signature. It is also a crime to knowingly buy, sell, keep, or hide such a check or security that is stolen or forged.
keyPoints: Forging or passing requires intent to defraud
Buying, selling, or keeping requires knowing it is stolen or forged
Lower penalty if total face value is $1,000 or less
510.penalty: A fine, up to 10 years in prison, or both; a fine, up to 1 year, or both if the total face value is $1,000 or less

511.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly remove, scratch off, tamper with, or change the identification number (VIN) on a motor vehicle or vehicle part. It is also a crime to tamper with an anti-theft decal or device on a vehicle to help steal it.

513.plain: It is a federal crime to make, pass, or possess a fake or forged security, such as a check, stock, bond, or money order, of a State, local government, or private organization, with intent to deceive. It is also a crime to make, have, or sell tools for making fake securities, intending them to be used that way.
keyPoints: Making, passing, or possessing requires intent to deceive
Tools crime requires intent that they be used to make fakes
Covers checks, stocks, bonds, money orders, and many other financial papers
513.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both

541.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly bring goods into the country by understating their weight or measure, giving a false description of their quality or value, or paying less import tax (duty) than is legally owed.

542.plain: It is a federal crime to bring or try to bring imported goods into U.S. commerce using false invoices, papers, or statements, or any fraudulent practice. It is also a crime to do any willful act that may cheat the government out of import taxes (duties).

Each offense can be fined separately

545.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly and willfully smuggle goods into the United States to cheat the government, or to use false papers at customs. Handling illegally imported goods requires knowing they were imported illegally

546.plain: It is a federal crime for owners or controllers of a U.S. ship to use or allow the ship to be used to smuggle goods into a foreign country against its laws. This also covers people on board who help, and renting out a ship when there is reason to believe it will be used for smuggling.

548.plain: It is a federal crime to fraudulently hide, remove, or repack goods stored in a bonded warehouse (a government-supervised warehouse for goods awaiting import taxes), or to change or wipe off the marks on packages there.

Breaking in must be malicious and with intent to remove goods
Receiving or moving goods requires knowing they were illegally removed

552.plain: It is a federal crime for a federal officer or employee to knowingly help anyone break laws against importing, advertising, selling, or mailing obscene materials or materials urging treason, rebellion, or threats to kill or harm people.

keyPoints: Must know the item is stolen or its ID number was altered

ID number exception for crash or fire damage or lawful changes

554.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly export, or try to export, any goods from the United States in violation of U.S. law or regulation. It is also a crime to buy, sell, hide, or help move such goods knowing they are meant to be exported illegally.

555.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly build or pay for an unauthorized tunnel under the U.S. border. 592.plain: It is a federal crime for a military officer or other federal employee to order, bring, or keep troops or armed men at a place where an election is being held. The only exception is when force is needed to fight off armed enemies of the United States.

594.plain: It is a federal crime to intimidate, threaten, or pressure someone, or try to, to interfere with their right to vote, or to make them vote or not vote for a federal candidate.

Attempts are covered

595.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
