596.plain: It is a federal crime to poll members of the armed forces about how they voted or plan to vote for a candidate, or to publish the results of such a poll.
keyPoints: Applies to anyone, inside or outside the military
A 'poll' means questions asked to compile answers
Publishing or releasing poll results is also covered
596.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: polls any member of such forces
states, publishes, or releases any result of any purported poll taken from or among the members of the Armed Forces of the United States

act: poll members of the armed forces about how they voted or plan to vote
publish the results of such a poll

597.plain: It is a federal crime to pay or offer to pay someone to vote, not vote, or vote for or against a candidate. It is also a crime to ask for or accept such payment in exchange for a vote.
keyPoints: Covers both giving and taking payment
Higher penalty if the violation was willful
597.penalty: A fine, up to 1 year in prison, or both; a fine, up to 2 years, or both if willful
acts: makes or offers to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote, or to vote for or against any candidate
solicits, accepts, or receives any such expenditure in consideration of his vote or the withholding of his vote

act: pay or offer to pay someone to vote, not vote, or vote for or against a candidate
ask for or accept such payment in exchange for a vote

598.plain: It is a federal crime to use federal relief or public-works money, or power given by such funding laws, to interfere with or pressure anyone in exercising the right to vote.
keyPoints: Covers federal work relief, relief, and public-works funds
Must be for the purpose of interfering with or coercing a voter
598.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: uses any part of any appropriation made by Congress for work relief, relief, or for increasing employment
exercises or administers any authority conferred by any Appropriation Act for the purpose of interfering with, restraining, or coercing any individual in the exercise of his right to vote

act: use federal relief or public-works money, or power given by such funding laws,
intent: to interfere with or pressure anyone in exercising the right to vote

599.plain: It is a federal crime for a candidate to promise someone a public or private job, or to promise to help them get one, in order to win support for the candidate's campaign.
keyPoints: Applies to candidates
Promise may be direct or indirect
Higher penalty if the violation was willful
599.penalty: A fine, up to 1 year in prison, or both; a fine, up to 2 years, or both if willful
acts: promises or pledges the appointment, or the use of his influence or support for the appointment of any person to any public or private position or employment

act: promise someone a public or private job, or to promise to help them get one
intent: in order to win support for the candidate's campaign

600.plain: It is a federal crime to promise anyone a job, contract, or other benefit paid for by a federal law as a reward for political activity or for supporting or opposing a candidate or party.
keyPoints: The benefit must be made possible at least partly by an Act of Congress
Covers general, special, and primary elections and party conventions
600.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: promises any employment, position, compensation, contract, appointment, or other benefit

act: promise anyone a job, contract, or other benefit paid for by a federal law
intent: as a reward for political activity

601.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly force or try to force someone to give to a candidate or political party by taking away, or threatening to take away, a government job or benefit that is funded at least partly by federal law.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Job or benefit must be funded at least partly by an Act of Congress
Covers federal, State, and local candidates
601.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: causes or attempts to cause any person to make a contribution of a thing of value (including services) for the benefit of any candidate or any political party

act: force or try to force someone to give to a candidate or political party

602.plain: It is a federal crime for members of Congress, congressional candidates, federal employees, or others paid from the U.S. Treasury to knowingly ask other federal workers or Treasury-paid people for political contributions.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Both the asker and the person asked must be in the covered groups
Some federal and postal employees are exempt unless other federal rules forbid the activity
602.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: solicit any contribution within the meaning of section 301(8) of the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 from any other such officer, employee, or person

act: ask other federal workers or Treasury-paid people for political contributions

603.plain: It is a federal crime for a federal employee, or someone paid from the U.S. Treasury, to give a political contribution to their own boss if the boss is a federal official or member of Congress.
keyPoints: The person receiving must be the giver's employer or employing authority
Giving to the boss's authorized campaign committee counts
Some federal and postal employees are exempt unless other federal rules forbid it
603.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: make any contribution within the meaning of section 301(8) of the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 to any other such officer, employee or person

act: give a political contribution to their own boss

604.plain: It is a federal crime to ask for or receive political contributions from someone known to be receiving federal relief or work-relief benefits.
keyPoints: Must know the person receives federal relief benefits
Covers being involved in any way in the asking or receiving
604.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: solicits or receives or is in any manner concerned in soliciting or receiving any assessment, subscription, or contribution for any political purpose

act: ask for or receive political contributions

605.plain: It is a federal crime to give lists or names of people receiving federal relief benefits to a political candidate or campaign for political purposes. It is also a crime to receive such lists for political purposes.
keyPoints: Must be for political purposes
Covers both giving and receiving the list
605.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: furnishes or discloses any list or names of persons receiving compensation, employment or benefits
receives any such list or names for political purposes

act: give lists or names of people receiving federal relief benefits
receive such lists for political purposes

606.plain: It is a federal crime for certain federal officials or employees to fire, demote, promote, or change the pay of another federal worker, or threaten or promise to, because that worker gave or refused to give a political contribution.
keyPoints: Applies to the federal officers and employees listed in section 602
Promises and threats count, not just actions
606.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: discharges, or promotes, or degrades, or in any manner changes the official rank or compensation of any other officer or employee
promises or threatens so to do

act: fire, demote, promote, or change the pay of another federal worker
threaten or promise to

607.plain: It is a federal crime to ask for or receive election donations from a person who is in a federal office building. It is also a crime for federal officials, including the President and members of Congress, to ask for or receive election donations while in such a building.
keyPoints: Applies to Federal, State, and local elections
Covers rooms or buildings used for official federal duties
Exception for some congressional and White House staff who forward contributions to a political committee within 7 days
607.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison, a fine of up to $5,000, or both
acts: to solicit or receive a donation of money or other thing of value in connection with a Federal, State, or local election

act: ask for or receive election donations from a person who is in a federal office building
ask for or receive election donations while in such a building

608.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly deny or try to deny military or overseas voters their rights under the federal absentee voting law. It is also a crime to give false information to make someone eligible to vote under that law, or to pay or accept payment for registering or voting.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Protects military members and U.S. citizens living overseas
Covers both offering and accepting payment
608.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: deprives or attempts to deprive any person of a right under the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act
gives false information for the purpose of establishing the eligibility of any person to register or vote
pays or offers to pay, or accepts payment for registering or voting under such Act

act: deny or try to deny military or overseas voters their rights
give false information to make someone eligible to vote
pay or accept payment for registering or voting

609.plain: It is a federal crime for a military officer to use military authority to influence how a service member votes, or to make service members march to a polling place, or to try to do so.
keyPoints: Applies to commissioned, noncommissioned, warrant, and petty officers
Attempts are covered
Free discussion of political issues and candidates is still allowed
609.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: uses military authority to influence the vote of a member of the Armed Forces
to require a member of the Armed Forces to march to a polling place

act: use military authority to influence how a service member votes
make service members march to a polling place

610.plain: It is a federal crime to intimidate, threaten, order, or pressure a federal employee, or try to, to take part or not take part in political activity, such as voting, donating, or campaigning.
keyPoints: Protects federal government employees
Attempts are covered
Covers voting, contributions, and campaign work
610.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: to intimidate, threaten, command, or coerce, or attempt to intimidate, threaten, command, or coerce, any employee of the Federal Government

act: intimidate, threaten, order, or pressure a federal employee

611.plain: It is a federal crime for a non-citizen to vote in an election for a federal office, such as President or Congress. Non-citizens may vote on local matters on the same ballot day only if State or local law allows it and the voting is kept separate from federal races.
keyPoints: Applies to non-citizens (aliens)
Exception if both parents are citizens, they lived here before age 16, and reasonably believed they were citizens
611.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: to vote in any election held solely or in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President

act: for a non-citizen to vote in an election for a federal office

641.plain: It is a federal crime to steal, embezzle (take money or property you were trusted with), or knowingly misuse or sell without permission money, records, or property of the U.S. government. It is also a crime to receive or keep such property knowing it was stolen, intending to use it for gain.
keyPoints: Covers government property and property being made under government contracts
Receiving or keeping requires knowing it was stolen or misused
Penalty depends on whether total value is over $1,000
641.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both; up to 1 year, a fine, or both if the total value is $1,000 or less
acts: embezzles, steals, purloins, or knowingly converts to his use or the use of another
sells, conveys or disposes of any record, voucher, money, or thing of value of the United States
receives, conceals, or retains the same with intent to convert it to his use or gain

act: steal, embezzle
misuse or sell without permission money, records, or property of the U.S. government
receive or keep such property
intent: intending to use it for gain

642.plain: It is a federal crime to steal, embezzle, or hide tools or materials the U.S. government uses to print money, stamps, bonds, and other official papers. This includes blank paper made for such documents and partly printed copies. It applies to anyone acting without government permission.
keyPoints: Must be done without authority from the United States
Covers printing tools and special paper
Covers partly printed or look-alike documents, whether or not meant to be used
642.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: secretes within, or embezzles, or takes and carries away from any building, room, office, apartment, vault, safe, or other place
so secretes, embezzles, or takes and carries away any paper, parchment, or other material prepared and intended to be used

act: steal, embezzle, or hide tools or materials

643.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime for a federal officer, employee, or agent who receives public money they are not allowed to keep as pay to fail to account for it as the law requires.
keyPoints: Applies to federal officers, employees, and agents
Money must be public money not owed to them as pay
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
643.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or a fine equal to the amount taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: fails to render his accounts for the same as provided by law

act: fail to account for it as the law requires

644.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime for someone who is not an approved holder of government money (such as a banker) to knowingly take public money as a deposit or loan from a federal officer, or to use public money for purposes the law does not allow.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Applies to people not authorized to hold public money
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
644.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or a fine up to the amount taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine of up to $1,000, or both
acts: receives from any disbursing officer, or collector of internal revenue, or other agent of the United States, any public money on deposit
uses, transfers, converts, appropriates, or applies any portion of the public money for any purpose not prescribed by law

act: take public money as a deposit or loan from a federal officer
use public money for purposes the law does not allow

645.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime for a federal court officer (such as a marshal, clerk, trustee, or their staff) to keep or use for themselves or someone else money they receive through their job, or to refuse to turn it over when asked.
keyPoints: Applies to federal court officers and their deputies and employees
Having a personal interest in the money is not a defense
Applies only if no other federal law punishes the act
645.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or up to double the amount taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: retains or converts to his own use or to the use of another
unlawfully retains any money coming into his hands by virtue of his official relation, position or employment

act: keep or use for themselves or someone else money they receive through their job
refuse to turn it over when asked

646.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime for a federal court clerk or officer to fail to promptly deposit court money with the Treasury or an approved depository, or to keep or use that money for themselves or others.
keyPoints: Applies to clerks and other federal court officers
Covers failing to deposit as well as personal use
Court-approved release of money on security is allowed
646.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or up to the amount taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: fails to deposit promptly any money belonging in the registry of the court
retains or converts to his own use or to the use of another any such money

act: fail to promptly deposit court money
keep or use that money for themselves or others

647.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime to knowingly accept money that belongs in a federal court's registry (funds the court holds) from a court clerk or officer, whether as a loan, deposit, or otherwise.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Applies to the person receiving the money, not just the officer
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
647.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or up to the amount taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: receives, from a clerk or other officer of a court of the United States, as a deposit, loan, or otherwise, any money belonging in the registry of such court

act: accept money that belongs in a federal court's registry

648.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime for a person legally responsible for safekeeping public money to lend it, use it, take it for themselves, put it in a bank, or exchange it, unless the law specifically allows that.
keyPoints: Applies to people charged by law with keeping public money safe
Exceptions only where specially allowed by law
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
648.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or a fine equal to the amount taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: loans, uses, or converts to his own use, or deposits in any bank
exchanges for other funds, except as specially allowed by law, any portion of the public moneys intrusted to him for safe-keeping

act: lend it, use it, take it for themselves, put it in a bank, or exchange it

649.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime for anyone holding U.S. government money to fail to deposit it with the Treasury or a public depository when properly ordered to by the Treasury, another agency head, or the Government Accountability Office. The section also makes several related embezzlement laws apply to everyone who keeps, moves, or pays out public money.
keyPoints: Failure must follow a proper order to deposit
Covers anyone holding or controlling U.S. money
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
649.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or a fine equal to the amount taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: fails to deposit it with the Treasurer or some public depositary of the United States

act: fail to deposit it with the Treasury or a public depository

650.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime for the Treasurer of the United States or any public depository to fail to keep safe the government money deposited with it.
keyPoints: Applies to the Treasurer and public depositories
Covers money deposited by government officers and others holding U.S. money
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
650.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or a fine equal to the amount taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: fails to keep safely all moneys deposited by any disbursing officer or disbursing agent

act: fail to keep safe the government money deposited with it

651.plain: It is a federal crime for an officer who pays out public money to accept or send in a receipt from a government creditor without having paid that creditor the full amount shown on it.
keyPoints: Applies to officers who pay out public money
Receipt shows more than was actually paid
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less withheld
651.penalty: Up to 2 years in prison, a fine (or double the amount withheld, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: accepts, receives, or transmits to the Government Accountability Office to be allowed in his favor any receipt or voucher from a creditor of the United States without having paid the full amount specified therein

act: accept or send in a receipt from a government creditor without having paid that creditor the full amount

652.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime for a person in charge of paying federal funds to pay a federal employee less than the law requires while making the employee sign a receipt for a larger amount.
keyPoints: Applies to people responsible for paying federal appropriations
Employee must be made to sign for more than they received
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
652.penalty: Up to 2 years in prison, a fine (or double the amount withheld, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: pays to any clerk or other employee of the United States, or of any department or agency thereof, a sum less than that provided by law
requires such employee to receipt or give a voucher for an amount greater than that actually paid to and received by him

act: pay a federal employee less than the law requires
making the employee sign a receipt for a larger amount

653.plain: It is a federal embezzlement crime for a federal disbursing officer (someone who pays out government money) to take public money for personal use, lend it, deposit it, or withdraw or move it for purposes the law does not allow.
keyPoints: Applies to disbursing officers and those acting as one
Use must not be authorized by law
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
653.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or up to the amount taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: in any manner converts to his own use, or loans with or without interest, or deposits in any place or in any manner, except as authorized by law, any public money intrusted to him
withdraws from the Treasury or any authorized depositary, or transfers, or applies, any portion of the public money intrusted to him

act: take public money for personal use, lend it, deposit it, or withdraw or move it

654.plain: It is a federal crime for a federal officer or employee to embezzle or wrongfully take for themselves money or property belonging to someone else that they got through their job or by claiming official authority.
keyPoints: Applies to federal officers and employees
Property belongs to another person, not the government
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
654.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine (or up to the value taken, if greater), or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: embezzles or wrongfully converts to his own use the money or property of another which comes into his possession or under his control

act: embezzle or wrongfully take for themselves money or property belonging to someone else

655.plain: It is a federal crime for a bank examiner or assistant examiner to steal or hide money or property held by a federally insured or Federal Reserve member bank, including from safe deposit boxes. It applies to public examiners appointed by federal or state authorities, but not to private examiners hired by a clearing house or a bank's directors.
keyPoints: Applies to public bank examiners, federal or state
Does not cover private examiners
Offender is barred from serving as a national bank or FDIC examiner
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
655.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both; plus removal from examiner office
acts: steals, or unlawfully takes, or unlawfully conceals any money, note, draft, bond, or security or any other property of value in the possession of any bank or banking institution

act: steal or hide money or property held by a federally insured or Federal Reserve member bank

656.plain: It is a federal crime for an officer, director, employee, or agent of a bank (such as a Federal Reserve bank, national bank, or FDIC-insured bank) or its receiver to embezzle, take, or willfully misuse the bank's money or money trusted to it.
keyPoints: Applies to anyone connected in any way with a covered bank
Misapplying funds must be willful
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
656.penalty: Up to 30 years in prison, a fine of up to $1,000,000, or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: embezzles, abstracts, purloins or willfully misapplies any of the moneys, funds or credits of such bank

act: embezzle, take, or willfully misuse the bank's money or money trusted to it

657.plain: It is a federal crime for anyone working for or connected with certain federal lending, credit, or insurance agencies and institutions (such as the FDIC, credit unions, federal home loan banks, or farm credit banks) to embezzle, take, or willfully misuse their money or property.
keyPoints: Applies to officers, employees, agents, and receivers
Covers credit unions, savings and loans, and federal lending agencies
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
657.penalty: Up to 30 years in prison, a fine of up to $1,000,000, or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: embezzles, abstracts, purloins or willfully misapplies any moneys, funds, credits, securities or other things of value belonging to such institution

act: embezzle, take, or willfully misuse their money or property

658.plain: It is a federal crime to hide, remove, sell off, or take for oneself property that is pledged as security to (or held by) certain federal farm credit agencies, with intent to cheat.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly and with intent to defraud
Covers property mortgaged or pledged to farm credit agencies
Lower penalty if value is $1,000 or less
658.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: conceals, removes, disposes of, or converts to his own use or to that of another, any property mortgaged or pledged to, or held by, the Farm Credit Administration

act: hide, remove, sell off, or take for oneself property

659.plain: It is a federal crime to steal, embezzle, or trick someone out of goods moving in an interstate or international shipment, or luggage carried by a common carrier (a company that transports goods or people for the public). It is also a crime to buy or keep such goods knowing they were stolen, or to carry them across state lines knowing they were stolen.
keyPoints: Goods must be part of an interstate or foreign shipment
Receiving or possessing requires knowing the goods were stolen
A state conviction or acquittal for the same act bars federal charges
Theft of pre-retail medical products is punished under section 670 unless this section's penalty is greater
659.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both; if less than $1,000, up to 3 years, a fine, or both; if pre-retail medical products are involved, punished under section 670 unless this section's penalty is greater
acts: embezzles, steals, or unlawfully takes, carries away, or conceals, or by fraud or deception obtains from any pipeline system, railroad car, wagon, motortruck, trailer, or other vehicle
buys or receives or has in his possession any such goods or chattels, knowing the same to have been embezzled or stolen
breaks into, steals, takes, carries away, or conceals any of the contents of such baggage
buys, receives, or has in his possession any such baggage or any article therefrom
embezzles, steals, or unlawfully takes by any fraudulent device, scheme, or game
buys, receives, or has in his possession any such money, baggage, goods, or chattels, knowing the same to have been embezzled or stolen
The carrying or transporting of any such money, freight, express, baggage, goods, or chattels in interstate or foreign commerce, knowing the same to have been stolen

act: steal, embezzle, or trick someone out of goods
buy or keep such goods
carry them across state lines

660.plain: It is a federal crime for a leader or officer of a common carrier company (a company that transports goods or people for the public), or an employee riding on its vehicles in interstate commerce, to embezzle, steal, or willfully misuse company money or property connected to that business.
keyPoints: Applies to carrier executives and on-board employees
Misuse must be willful or knowing
A state conviction or acquittal for the same act bars federal charges
660.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: embezzles, steals, abstracts, or willfully misapplies, or willfully permits to be misapplied, any of the moneys, funds, credits, securities, property, or assets of such firm
converts the same to his own use or to the use of another

act: embezzle, steal, or willfully misuse company money or property

661.plain: It is a federal crime to steal someone's personal property in places under special federal control (such as federal lands, military bases, or U.S. ships at sea).
keyPoints: Must intend to steal
Higher penalty if worth over $1,000 or taken directly from a person
For stolen IOUs or written debts, value is the amount owed
661.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both if over $1,000 or taken from a person; otherwise up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: takes and carries away, with intent to steal or purloin, any personal property of another

act: steal someone's personal property

662.plain: It is a federal crime, in places under special federal control (such as federal lands or U.S. ships at sea), to buy, receive, or hide money or property knowing it was stolen or embezzled.
keyPoints: Must know the property was stolen or embezzled
Must occur within special federal jurisdiction
Lower penalty if $1,000 or less
662.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison, a fine, or both; if $1,000 or less, up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: buys, receives, or conceals any money, goods, bank notes, or other thing which may be the subject of larceny

act: buy, receive, or hide money or property

663.plain: It is a federal crime to ask for donations by claiming they are for the U.S. government while planning to steal or misuse them. It is also a crime to steal or misuse money or property donated to the United States.
keyPoints: Asking for gifts must be done with intent to steal or misuse them
Covers anyone holding property donated for U.S. use
663.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: solicits any gift of money or other property, and represents that such gift is being solicited for the use of the United States
embezzles, steals or purloins such money or property, or converts the same to any other use or purpose

act: ask for donations by claiming they are for the U.S. government
steal or misuse money or property donated to the United States
intent: while planning to steal or misuse them

664.plain: It is a federal crime to embezzle, steal, or willfully take money or property belonging to an employee benefit or pension plan covered by the federal ERISA law (a law governing workplace benefit plans).
keyPoints: Applies to anyone, not just plan officials
Taking or converting must be unlawful and willful
Covers welfare and pension plans and related funds
664.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: embezzles, steals, or unlawfully and willfully abstracts or converts to his own use or to the use of another, any of the moneys, funds, securities, premiums, credits, property, or other assets of any employee welfare benefit plan

act: embezzle, steal, or willfully take money or property

665.plain: It is a federal crime for people connected with federally funded job-training programs to knowingly enroll ineligible people or to steal or misuse program funds. It is also a crime to pressure someone into giving up money by threatening their job in such a program, or to willfully obstruct an investigation of the program.
keyPoints: Covers Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act and Workforce Investment Act funds
Theft or misuse: lower penalty if $1,000 or less
Obstruction must be willful
665.penalty: Theft or misuse: up to 2 years in prison, a fine, or both (up to 1 year if $1,000 or less); job threats or obstructing investigations: up to 1 year, a fine, or both
acts: enrolls an ineligible participant
embezzles, willfully misapplies, steals, or obtains by fraud any of the moneys, funds, assets, or property
induces any person to give up any money or thing of any value to any person
obstructs or impedes or willfully endeavors to obstruct or impede, an investigation or inquiry

act: enroll ineligible people
steal or misuse program funds
pressure someone into giving up money by threatening their job
obstruct an investigation of the program

666.plain: It is a federal crime for an agent of an organization or state, local, or tribal government that gets over $10,000 a year in federal funds to steal or misuse $5,000 or more of its property, or to take bribes tied to deals worth $5,000 or more. It is also a crime to offer or pay such bribes.
keyPoints: Organization must receive over $10,000 in federal benefits in a one-year period
Property or deal must be worth $5,000 or more
Bribery must be done corruptly, intending to influence or reward

700.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly burn, cut up, deface, dirty, trample, or keep on the floor or ground a U.S. flag. Properly disposing of a worn or dirty flag is allowed. The section also lets court rulings on its constitutionality be appealed directly to the Supreme Court.

709.plain: It is a federal crime to use names, words, or symbols that falsely suggest a business is a federal agency or is backed by the government. 922.plain: This section lists the main federal gun crimes. It is a federal crime for certain people to have guns or ammunition, including people convicted of crimes punishable by more than a year in prison, fugitives, illegal drug users, people under certain domestic-violence restraining orders, and people convicted of domestic-violence misdemeanors. It is also a crime to sell guns to such people, deal in guns without a license, lie when buying a gun, have stolen guns or guns with removed serial numbers, have or transfer most machineguns, or knowingly have a gun in a school zone. Licensed dealers must follow rules such as age limits, record-keeping, and running background checks before most sales.

It also makes it a federal crime to use, carry, or have a gun during a violent crime or drug trafficking crime, or to plan with others to do so. It also covers stealing guns, smuggling guns, traveling to another state to get a gun for a crime, and buying or transferring guns knowing or having reason to believe they will be used in serious crimes. 925.plain: This section lists exceptions to the federal gun laws, such as guns used by government agencies and certain guns for members of the military serving overseas. It also lets people who are barred from having guns ask the Attorney General for relief, and says which guns may be brought into the country.

925A.plain: This section lets a person who was wrongly denied a gun after a background check sue the government responsible to fix the wrong information or approve the sale. The court may make the losing side pay the winner's lawyer fees.

925B.plain: This section requires the Attorney General to tell local police, and when practical local prosecutors, within 24 hours when the federal background check system blocks someone from getting a gun. If the FBI later finds the person was not actually barred, those officials must be told.

925C.plain: This section requires the Attorney General to send Congress a yearly report on gun background-check denials, broken down by federal court district. The report covers numbers of denials, appeals, investigations, charges, and convictions.

925D.plain: This section lets the Attorney General appoint state, tribal, and local prosecutors and deputize local officers to help enforce federal gun bans for people under domestic-violence restraining orders or with domestic-violence convictions. It also requires focusing these efforts on at least 75 areas with high rates of gun violence against intimate partners.

926.plain: This section lets the Attorney General make rules needed to carry out the federal gun laws in this chapter, after 90 days' public notice and a chance for hearings. It forbids rules that would create a federal registry of guns, gun owners, or gun sales, or move dealers' records to government facilities.

926A.plain: This section lets a person who may legally have a gun carry it through any place, even where local law would forbid it, when traveling between two places where they may legally have it. The gun must be unloaded and not reachable from the passenger area; in vehicles without a trunk, it must be in a locked container other than the glove box or console.

926B.plain: This section lets qualified, active law enforcement officers carrying their agency photo ID carry a concealed gun anywhere in the country, despite state or local laws. It does not override laws letting private owners or state and local governments ban guns on their property, and it excludes machine guns, silencers, and destructive devices.

926C.plain: This section lets qualified retired law enforcement officers carry a concealed gun anywhere in the country if they carry the required photo ID and proof of passing firearms qualification within the past year. It sets conditions such as at least 10 years of service (or a service-related disability), good standing, and no mental-health disqualification.

927.plain: This section says federal gun laws do not push aside state gun laws on the same subject, unless the two directly conflict and cannot both be followed.

928.plain: This section says that if a court strikes down any part of this chapter of gun laws, the rest of the chapter still stays in effect.

929.plain: It is a federal crime to use or carry a gun while having armor-piercing ammunition that fits it, during and in relation to a federal crime of violence or drug trafficking crime. This adds a separate prison sentence on top of the punishment for the underlying crime.
keyPoints: Must be during and in relation to a federal violent or drug trafficking crime
Must use or carry a gun and possess armor-piercing ammunition for it

981.plain: This section lets the federal government take property (called civil forfeiture) that is linked to certain crimes, such as money laundering, counterfeiting, bank fraud, and some foreign offenses, even without a criminal conviction of the owner. It also explains how such property is seized, held, and used, and includes special rules for bank accounts at foreign banks.

982.plain: This section requires a court, when sentencing someone convicted of certain crimes (such as money laundering, bank fraud, counterfeiting, car theft, immigration document crimes, health care fraud, and telemarketing fraud), to order that person to give up (forfeit) property tied to the crime. It also sets the procedures that govern this criminal forfeiture.

983.plain: This section sets the general rules for civil forfeiture (when the government sues to take property linked to a crime). It covers notice deadlines, how owners file claims, the government's burden of proof, the innocent-owner defense, release of seized property, and limits on forfeitures that are grossly out of proportion to the offense.

984.plain: This section lets the government take cash, bank funds, or precious metals in a civil forfeiture case without tracing the exact money used in the crime, as long as identical property is in the same place or account. Such cases must be started within 1 year of the offense, with special limits for accounts between banks.

985.plain: This section sets the rules for civil forfeiture of land and buildings. The government must go through court, generally cannot seize the property or evict owners before a forfeiture order, and must give notice unless a court finds an emergency.

986.plain: This section lets parties in certain money-laundering and drug-related forfeiture cases get subpoenas (court orders to hand over documents) for bank records. A claimant who refuses to provide foreign bank records they could obtain can face court sanctions, including dismissal of their claim.

987.plain: This section lets owners challenge the confiscation of property taken under laws targeting suspected international terrorists, including by showing they are innocent owners. Courts may consider normally inadmissible evidence if it is reliable and needed to protect national security.

1152.plain: Extends general federal criminal laws for federal areas to Indian country, except for crimes by one Indian against another, Indians already punished by tribal law, or cases where treaties give tribes exclusive control.

If federal law does not define one of these crimes, the law of the state where it happened applies.

Penalty depends on whether goods total $1,000 or more

If the offender cannot pay or is not caught, the U.S. Treasury pays, unless the owner or the owner's tribe sought revenge by force.

1161.plain: This section limits where certain federal Indian liquor laws apply. They do not apply outside Indian country, or to alcohol activity in Indian country that follows both State law and a tribal ordinance approved by the Secretary of the Interior and published in the Federal Register.

1162.plain: This section gives Alaska, California, Minnesota, Nebraska, Oregon, and Wisconsin power to enforce their criminal laws in most Indian country within their borders, with some listed exceptions. It protects tribal trust property and hunting and fishing rights, and lets a tribe ask, with the Attorney General's consent, for federal jurisdiction to apply again alongside State jurisdiction.

1163.plain: It is a federal crime to embezzle, steal, or misuse money or property belonging to an Indian tribal organization or held by its officers or employees. It is also a crime to knowingly receive, hide, or keep such property to use it.

Receiving the property requires knowing it was stolen or misused

1363.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully and maliciously destroy or damage any building, vehicle, or other property in areas under special federal control (such as federal lands and U.S. ships). Trying or planning with others to do so is also a crime.

Applies only in special federal areas (special maritime and territorial jurisdiction)
Harsher penalty if the building is a home or a life is put in danger

acts: destroys or injures any structure, conveyance, or other real or personal property

act: destroy or damage any building, vehicle, or other property

1364.plain: It is a federal crime to use fire or explosives to damage or destroy goods being exported from the United States, or the places where those goods are kept, in order to block or interfere with the export.
keyPoints: Must intend to prevent or interfere with exports
Damage must be done by fire or explosives

1365.plain: It is a federal crime to tamper, or try to tamper, with consumer products like food, drugs, or cosmetics, or their labels or containers, with reckless disregard for the risk of death or injury. It is also a crime to taint products to hurt a business, to knowingly spread false claims that a product was tainted, to knowingly threaten tampering, or to conspire to tamper. keyPoints: Main offense requires extreme indifference to risk of death or injury
Harsher punishment if someone is seriously injured or killed
False tampering claims and threats must be believable
Inserting writings into products is punished more harshly after a prior conviction

1366.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly and willfully damage the property of an energy facility, such as a power plant, fuel storage site, or power line. Attempts are also covered, and conspiracies are covered for the more serious version. Nuclear facilities regulated by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and interstate gas pipelines are not covered.

Harsher punishment if someone dies

1367.plain: It is a federal crime to intentionally or maliciously interfere with the operation of a communications or weather satellite, or to block or disrupt satellite transmissions, without the operator's permission.
keyPoints: Must be intentional or malicious
Must be without the satellite operator's authority
Lawful law enforcement and intelligence activities are not covered
1367.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison and/or a fine

1368.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully and maliciously harm a police dog or horse used by a federal agency. Trying or planning with others to do so is also a crime.
keyPoints: Must be willful and malicious
Protects dogs and horses used by federal agencies for law enforcement
Harsher punishment if the animal is killed, permanently disabled, disfigured, or seriously injured

1369.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully damage or destroy a monument, statue, plaque, or other structure on public property that honors people who served in the U.S. armed forces. The crime applies when the memorial is on federal property or the offender crosses state lines or uses the mail or interstate commerce.
keyPoints: Must be done willfully
Covers attempts
Memorial must be on public property
Needs a federal link: federal property, interstate travel, or mail/interstate commerce
1369.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison and/or a fine
acts: injures or destroys, or attempts to injure or destroy, any structure, plaque, statue, or other monument on public property

act: damage or destroy a monument, statue, plaque, or other structure

1381.plain: It is a federal crime to persuade or help a member of the U.S. Armed Forces (or a new recruit) to desert. It is also a crime to hide or protect a known deserter, or to refuse to hand one over when an authorized officer demands it.

Hiding a deserter requires knowing the person deserted
Refusing to turn over a deserter on an officer's demand is covered

Or reentry after being removed or ordered to stay away

Renting a place requires knowing or having good reason to know its use
Does not give military personnel power to arrest or search civilians

1385.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully use the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, or Space Force to enforce laws (for example, as a posse comitatus, meaning a group called to help law enforcement). This applies unless the Constitution or an Act of Congress expressly allows it.
keyPoints: Must be done willfully
Exception when the Constitution or Congress expressly authorizes it

1386.plain: It is a federal crime to steal, counterfeit, or unlawfully possess locks or keys that the Department of Defense uses to protect weapons, explosives, or classified information. It is also a crime for lock makers or contractors to give such locks or keys to unauthorized people.

Possession is a crime only with intent to misuse, sell, or dispose of it unlawfully
Contractors may only deliver to authorized people

Victims and the Attorney General can also sue for money damages.
keyPoints: Must be done willfully and with intent to disturb or block

Former members protected for 5 years after discharge

1421.plain: It is a federal crime for a court clerk or other official responsible for money collected in citizenship, naturalization, or alien registration proceedings to willfully fail to account for or pay that money to the United States. Conspiracy to commit child or forced sex trafficking (section 1591) has its own penalty
Property used in or earned from the crime must be forfeited

1595.plain: This section lets trafficking victims sue the offender, or anyone who knowingly profited from the trafficking, in federal court for damages and attorney fees. It sets a 10-year deadline to sue and lets State attorneys general sue for residents in sex trafficking cases.

1595A.plain: This section lets the U.S. Attorney General ask a federal court to order a person to stop (an injunction) ongoing or planned trafficking or related sex crimes. It sets court procedures, including keeping the case sealed while an indictment is secret.

1596.plain: This section lets U.S. courts handle certain slavery and trafficking crimes committed outside the United States if the offender is a U.S. citizen, a permanent resident, or present in the U.S. It limits prosecution if another country already prosecuted the person, unless top Justice Department officials approve.

1597.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly destroy, hide, take, or hold another person's passport or immigration document while committing, or to commit, certain immigration or visa fraud crimes, or to control that person's labor without legal authority. Interfering with enforcement

Must occur on the high seas

A treaty between the U.S. and the offender's country must declare the acts piracy

Taking must be meant to obstruct mail or pry into private affairs
