sells or offers to sell any such postage stamp, stamped envelope, or postal card
removes from any mail matter any stamp attached thereto in payment of postage
uses in payment of postage, any postage stamp, postal card, or stamped envelope, issued in pursuance of law, which has already been used for a like purpose

act: reuse canceled postage stamps
remove cancellation marks
remove a stamp from any mail
penalty: Postal Service employees face a higher penalty

1721.plain: It is a federal crime for a Postal Service officer or employee to misuse stamps, stamped envelopes, or postal cards in their care. This includes using them to pay debts or buy goods, selling them for more or less than face value, selling them outside their post office's area, or inflating post office receipts to raise their own pay.
keyPoints: Applies only to Postal Service officers and employees
Must be done knowingly and willfully
1721.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: uses or disposes of postage stamps, stamped envelopes, or postal cards entrusted to his care or custody in the payment of debts
pledges or hypothecates the same or sells or disposes of them except for cash
sells or disposes of postage stamps or postal cards for any larger or less sum than the values indicated on their faces
sells or disposes of stamped envelopes for a larger or less sum than is charged therefor by the Postal Service
sells or disposes of postage stamps, stamped envelopes, or postal cards at any point or place outside of the delivery of the office
inflates or induces the inflation of the receipts of any post office
sells or disposes of postage stamps, stamped envelopes, or postal cards, otherwise than as provided by law or the regulations of the Postal Service

act: misuse stamps, stamped envelopes, or postal cards in their care
selling them for more or less than face value
inflating post office receipts

1722.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly give the Postal Service false evidence about a publication to get it the cheaper second-class (periodicals) mailing rate.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Purpose must be to get the second-class rate
acts: submits to the Postal Service or to any officer or employee of the Postal Service, any false evidence relative to any publication

act: give the Postal Service false evidence about a publication
intent: to get it the cheaper second-class (periodicals) mailing rate

1723.plain: Lower-class mail with extra writing or printing added must pay the first-class rate. It is a federal crime to knowingly hide higher-class mail inside lower-class mail to pay a cheaper rate.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
The goal is to pay less postage than the higher class requires
acts: conceals or incloses any matter of a higher class in that of a lower class, and deposits the same for conveyance by mail, at a less rate

act: hide higher-class mail inside lower-class mail

1724.plain: This section lets the Postal Service require ships going between the U.S. and foreign ports to carry mail for set pay. If a ship's captain refuses, port officials must hold back the ship's permission to leave until the mail is accepted or no longer needed.

1725.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly and willfully put unstamped mail, such as bills, flyers, or account statements, into a mailbox approved by the Postal Service to avoid paying postage.
keyPoints: Must be knowing and willful
Must intend to avoid paying postage
Each piece can be a separate offense
acts: deposits any mailable matter such as statements of accounts, circulars, sale bills, or other like matter, on which no postage has been paid, in any letter box

act: put unstamped mail, such as bills, flyers, or account statements, into a mailbox

1726.plain: It is a federal crime for a postmaster or other person authorized to collect postage to fraudulently charge or accept a postage rate different from what the law sets, or any tip or reward.
keyPoints: Applies to postmasters and others authorized to collect postage
Must be done fraudulently
1726.penalty: Up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both
acts: fraudulently demands or receives any rate of postage or gratuity or reward other than is provided by law

act: charge or accept a postage rate different from what the law sets

1728.plain: It is a federal crime to put things in the mail during the official weighing period to make the mail heavier, intending to increase what a railroad mail carrier gets paid.
keyPoints: Must be done during the regular weighing period
Must intend to increase the carrier's pay
1728.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: places any matter in the mails during the regular weighing period, for the purpose of increasing the weight of the mail

act: put things in the mail during the official weighing period
intent: intending to increase what a railroad mail carrier gets paid

1729.plain: It is a federal crime to set up or claim to run a business or office using the sign, name, or title "post office" without Postal Service permission.
keyPoints: Applies only without Postal Service authority
Covers using the sign, name, or title "post office"
acts: sets up or professes to keep any office or place of business bearing the sign, name, or title of post office

act: set up or claim to run a business or office using the sign, name, or title "post office"

1730.plain: It is a federal crime for someone who is not part of the Postal Service's letter-carrier branch to wear the uniform or badge of a letter carrier.
keyPoints: Applies to people not connected to the letter-carrier branch
Exception: actors portraying mail carriers in plays, TV, or movies
1730.penalty: Up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both
acts: wears the uniform or badge which may be prescribed by the Postal Service to be worn by letter carriers

act: wear the uniform or badge of a letter carrier

1731.plain: It is a federal crime to put the words "United States Mail" (or similar words) on a ship, car, or other vehicle that does not actually carry mail. It is also a crime to falsely advertise that a vehicle carries mail.
keyPoints: Vehicle must not actually be used to carry mail
Owners, lessees, or operators who allow the violation are also covered
1731.penalty: Up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both
acts: to paint, print, or in any manner to place upon or attach to any steamboat or other vessel
the words "United States Mail", or any words, letters, or characters of like import
to give notice, by publishing in any newspaper or otherwise
is used in carrying the mail, when the same is not actually so used
suffers, or permits the violation of, any provision of this section

act: put the words "United States Mail" (or similar words) on a ship, car, or other vehicle
falsely advertise that a vehicle carries mail

1732.plain: It is a federal crime for a postmaster to approve a bidder's bond or certify sureties (people who guarantee a contract) before the bond or contract is signed. It is also a crime to knowingly or carelessly approve a bond backed by insufficient sureties, or to knowingly make a false certificate.
keyPoints: Applies to postmasters
Approving insufficient sureties can be knowing or without due care
Offender must also be removed and barred from being a postmaster
1732.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both; plus removal from office
acts: affixes his signature to the approval of any bond of a bidder
approves any bond of a bidder with insufficient sureties
makes any false or fraudulent certificate

act: approve a bidder's bond or certify sureties
approve a bond backed by insufficient sureties
make a false certificate
penalty: Offender must also be removed and barred from being a postmaster

1733.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly mail a periodical (like a magazine or newspaper) without prepaying postage, unless the law allows it. Postal employees who knowingly allow this are also covered.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Exception: when allowed by law
Applies to mailers and to postal workers who permit it
1733.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: mails any periodical publication without the prepayment of postage
permits any periodical publication to be mailed without prepayment of postage

act: mail a periodical (like a magazine or newspaper) without prepaying postage

1734.plain: It is a federal crime for an editor or publisher to print paid content in a second-class mail publication without clearly labeling it "advertisement."
keyPoints: Applies to editors and publishers
The content was paid for or payment was promised
acts: prints in a publication entered as second class mail, editorial or other reading matter for which he has been paid or promised a valuable consideration, without plainly marking the same "advertisement"

act: print paid content in a second-class mail publication without clearly labeling it "advertisement."

1735.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully mail sexually oriented advertisements in violation of the federal law that lets people opt out of receiving them (39 U.S.C. 3010). It is also a crime to sell, rent, or misuse the government's list of people who opted out.
keyPoints: Mailing violation must be willful
Covers misuse of the government-kept opt-out list
Repeat offenses carry a higher penalty
1735.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both; up to 10 years for a repeat offense
acts: uses the mails for the mailing, carriage in the mails, or delivery of any sexually oriented advertisement in violation of section 3010 of title 39
willfully violates any regulations of the Board of Governors issued under such section
sells, leases, rents, lends, exchanges, or licenses the use of
uses a mailing list maintained by the Board of Governors under such section

act: mail sexually oriented advertisements
sell, rent, or misuse the government's list
penalty: Repeat offenses carry a higher penalty

1736.plain: This section says that information a person gives, or actions they take, to comply with the federal sexually oriented mail law (39 U.S.C. 3010) generally cannot be used as evidence against them in a criminal case. The exception is a prosecution for giving false information.

1737.plain: It is a federal crime to print, copy, or make sexually related mail material while intending or knowing that it will be mailed in violation of federal laws on sexually oriented mail (39 U.S.C. 3008 or 3010).
keyPoints: Must intend or know the material will be mailed illegally
Repeat offenses carry a higher penalty
1737.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both; up to 10 years for a repeat offense
acts: print, reproduce, or manufacture any sexually related mail matter

act: print, copy, or make sexually related mail material
intent: intending or knowing that it will be mailed
penalty: Repeat offenses carry a higher penalty

1751.plain: It is a federal crime to kill, kidnap, attempt to kill or kidnap, conspire to kill or kidnap, or assault the President, President-elect, Vice President, Vice President-elect, an acting President, or certain senior White House and Vice President's office staff. The FBI investigates, and the crime is covered even if committed outside the U.S.
keyPoints: Government need not prove the attacker knew who the victim was
Killing is punished under the federal murder and manslaughter laws (sections 1111 and 1112)
Death possible for kidnapping or conspiracy if the victim dies
Assault with a weapon or causing injury raises staff-assault penalty
1751.penalty: Killing: punished under sections 1111 and 1112; kidnapping, attempt, or conspiracy: any term of years up to life, or death if the victim dies; assault: up to 10 years (up to 1 year for staff unless a weapon or injury) and a fine
acts: kills (1) any individual who is the President of the United States
kidnaps any individual designated in subsection (a) of this section
attempts to kill or kidnap any individual designated in subsection (a) of this section
conspire to kill or kidnap any individual designated in subsection (a) of this section
assaults any person designated in subsection (a)(1)
assaults any person designated in subsection (a)(2)

act: kill, kidnap, attempt to kill or kidnap, conspire to kill or kidnap, or assault

1752.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly enter or stay in a restricted area without permission, such as the White House grounds or a place where the President or another Secret Service-protected person is visiting. It is also a crime to disrupt government business there, block entrances, commit violence, or fly a drone into or over it. Attempts and conspiracies are covered.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly; disruption and blocking require intent to disrupt government business
Restricted area must be posted, cordoned off, or otherwise restricted
Higher penalty if a weapon is used or carried, or significant bodily injury results
1752.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both; up to 10 years if a weapon is involved or significant injury results
acts: enters or remains in any restricted building or grounds without lawful authority to do so
engages in disorderly or disruptive conduct in, or within such proximity to, any restricted building or grounds
obstructs or impedes ingress or egress to or from any restricted building or grounds
engages in any act of physical violence against any person or property in any restricted building or grounds
operates an unmanned aircraft system
attempts or conspires to do so

act: enter or stay in a restricted area without permission
disrupt government business there, block entrances, commit violence, or fly a drone into or over it

1761.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly transport goods made by prisoners across state lines or import them into the U.S.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Does not cover goods made by people on parole, probation, or supervised release
Exceptions: farm goods, goods made for government use, and approved prison work pilot projects with fair wages
1761.penalty: Up to 2 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: transports in interstate commerce or from any foreign country into the United States any goods, wares, or merchandise manufactured, produced, or mined, wholly or in part by convicts or prisoners

act: transport goods made by prisoners across state lines or import them into the U.S.

1762.plain: Packages of prisoner-made goods shipped between states or countries must be clearly marked with the shipper, receiver, contents, and the prison where they were made. It is a federal crime to break this rule, and the goods can be taken by the government.
keyPoints: Applies to goods made wholly or partly by prisoners
Goods shipped illegally under this section or section 1761 are forfeited
1762.penalty: A fine; the goods can be forfeited (taken by the government)
acts: shall be plainly and clearly marked
violates this section

act: break this rule
penalty: the goods can be taken by the government

1791.plain: It is a federal crime to give or try to give a prohibited item to a federal prison inmate in violation of law or prison rules. It is also a crime for an inmate to make, have, or get such an item. Prohibited items include weapons, drugs, alcohol, money, cell phones, and anything that threatens prison safety.
keyPoints: Penalty depends on the type of item
Hard drugs like narcotics, meth, LSD, or PCP carry the highest penalty
Inmate sentences must run after their current sentence
Covers federal prisons and facilities holding people for the Attorney General
1791.penalty: A fine or prison, depending on the item: up to 20 years (hard drugs), 10 (guns, schedule I/II drugs), 5 (marijuana, other weapons), 1 (other drugs, alcohol, cash, phones), or 6 months (other dangerous items)
acts: provides to an inmate of a prison a prohibited object, or attempts to do so
makes, possesses, or obtains, or attempts to make or obtain, a prohibited object

act: give or try to give a prohibited item to a federal prison inmate
make, have, or get such an item

1792.plain: It is a federal crime to start, plot, try to cause, help, or conspire to cause a mutiny or riot at a federal prison, jail, or detention center.
keyPoints: Applies to federal penal, detention, or correctional facilities
Attempts must be willful
1792.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: instigates, connives, willfully attempts to cause, assists, or conspires to cause any mutiny or riot, at any Federal penal, detention, or correctional facility

act: start, plot, try to cause, help, or conspire to cause a mutiny or riot

1793.plain: It is a federal crime to go onto land or a facility belonging to the Bureau of Prisons without permission or legal authority.
keyPoints: Applies only without lawful authority or permission
Covers Bureau of Prisons reservations, land, and facilities
1793.penalty: Up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both
acts: goes upon a reservation, land, or a facility of the Bureau of Prisons

act: go onto land or a facility belonging to the Bureau of Prisons without permission

1801.plain: It is a federal crime, on federal land or other places under special federal jurisdiction, to knowingly photograph, film, or broadcast images of someone's private areas without consent. This applies where the person would reasonably expect privacy.
keyPoints: Must intend to capture the image and do so knowingly
Victim must not consent and have a reasonable expectation of privacy
Applies only in federal maritime and territorial jurisdiction
Lawful police, prison, or intelligence work is exempt
1801.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: has the intent to capture an image of a private area of an individual without their consent
does so under circumstances in which the individual has a reasonable expectation of privacy

act: photograph, film, or broadcast images of someone's private areas without consent
intent: Must intend to capture the image

1831.plain: It is a federal crime to steal, copy, send, receive, or possess a trade secret (valuable confidential business information) without permission, when the person intends or knows it will benefit a foreign government or foreign agent. Attempts and conspiracies are also covered.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Must intend or know it will benefit a foreign government, agency, or agent
Organizations face much larger fines
1831.penalty: Up to 15 years in prison, a fine up to $5,000,000, or both; organizations can be fined up to $10,000,000 or 3 times the secret's value
acts: steals, or without authorization appropriates, takes, carries away, or conceals, or by fraud, artifice, or deception obtains a trade secret

without authorization copies, duplicates, sketches, draws, photographs, downloads, uploads, alters, destroys, photocopies, replicates, transmits, delivers, sends, mails, communicates, or conveys a trade secret
receives, buys, or possesses a trade secret, knowing the same to have been stolen or appropriated, obtained, or converted without authorization
attempts to commit any offense described in any of paragraphs (1) through (3)
conspires with one or more other persons to commit any offense described in any of paragraphs (1) through (3)

act: steal, copy, send, receive, or possess a trade secret
intent: intends or knows it will benefit a foreign government or foreign agent

1832.plain: It is a federal crime to steal, copy, send, receive, or possess someone's trade secret (valuable confidential business information) without permission, to benefit someone other than the owner. The secret must relate to a product or service in interstate or international commerce. Attempts and conspiracies are also covered.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Must intend or know the act will harm the owner
Organizations face fines up to $5,000,000 or 3 times the secret's value
1832.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both; organizations can be fined up to $5,000,000 or 3 times the secret's value
acts: steals, or without authorization appropriates, takes, carries away, or conceals, or by fraud, artifice, or deception obtains such information

without authorization copies, duplicates, sketches, draws, photographs, downloads, uploads, alters, destroys, photocopies, replicates, transmits, delivers, sends, mails, communicates, or conveys such information
receives, buys, or possesses such information, knowing the same to have been stolen or appropriated, obtained, or converted without authorization
attempts to commit any offense described in paragraphs (1) through (3)
conspires with one or more other persons to commit any offense described in paragraphs (1) through (3)

act: steal, copy, send, receive, or possess someone's trade secret
intent: to benefit someone other than the owner
Must intend or know the act will harm the owner

1833.plain: This section says the trade secret laws do not cover lawful government activity. It also protects people from criminal or civil liability when they share a trade secret in confidence with officials or a lawyer to report a suspected crime, or in a sealed court filing, and requires employers to tell employees about this protection.

1834.plain: This section says that forfeiture (taking property), destruction of goods, and restitution (paying victims back) for trade secret crimes follow the rules in section 2323.

1835.plain: This section requires courts to protect the secrecy of trade secrets during trade secret cases, and lets the government appeal an order to disclose one. It also lets owners explain privately why information should stay secret, and says sharing it during a prosecution does not give up its protection.

1836.plain: This section lets the Attorney General, and owners of stolen trade secrets (valuable business information kept secret), sue in federal civil court. It sets rules for emergency court seizures of property, the money damages and court orders a court can give, and a 3-year deadline to sue.

1837.plain: This section says the federal trade secret laws also cover conduct outside the United States if the offender is a U.S. citizen, permanent resident, or U.S. organization, or if any act helping the offense happened in the United States.

1838.plain: This section says the federal trade secret laws do not replace other federal or state civil or criminal remedies for trade secret theft, except as stated in section 1833(b). It also does not limit lawful release of information by government employees under the Freedom of Information Act.

1841.plain: It is a separate federal crime to kill or injure an unborn child while committing one of certain listed federal crimes. The punishment is generally the same as if the harm had happened to the mother. If the person intentionally kills or tries to kill the unborn child, the federal murder and manslaughter laws apply instead.
keyPoints: Must happen during one of the listed federal crimes
No proof needed that the offender knew she was pregnant or meant to harm the child
Does not apply to consented abortions, medical treatment, or the pregnant woman herself
The death penalty cannot be imposed
1841.penalty: Same punishment as if the harm had been done to the mother; intentional killing is punished under sections 1111, 1112, and 1113; no death penalty
acts: engages in conduct that violates any of the provisions of law listed in subsection (b)
thereby causes the death of, or bodily injury (as defined in section 1365) to, a child, who is in utero
intentionally kills or attempts to kill the unborn child

act: kill or injure an unborn child while committing one of certain listed federal crimes
intentionally kills or tries to kill the unborn child
penalty: The death penalty cannot be imposed

1851.plain: It is a federal crime to mine or remove coal from land owned or reserved by the United States, intending to wrongfully take, sell, or get rid of it.
keyPoints: Coal must come from U.S. government land
Must intend to wrongfully take, sell, or dispose of the coal
Does not affect rights given by other federal laws
1851.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: mines or removes coal of any character, whether anthracite, bituminous, or lignite, from beds or deposits in lands of, or reserved to the United States

act: mine or remove coal from land owned or reserved by the United States
intent: intending to wrongfully take, sell, or get rid of it

1852.plain: It is a federal crime to cut or recklessly destroy timber growing on U.S. public lands, or to remove such timber to export or sell it. It is also a crime for owners or operators of vessels, vehicles, aircraft, or railroads to knowingly transport that timber or lumber made from it.
keyPoints: Transporters must act knowingly
Miners and farmers may clear their own claims or land and use needed timber
Does not affect rights to cut timber under other federal laws
1852.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: cuts, or wantonly destroys any timber growing on the public lands of the United States
removes any timber from said public lands, with intent to export or to dispose of the same
transports any timber so cut or removed from said lands, or lumber manufactured therefrom

act: cut or recklessly destroy timber growing on U.S. public lands
remove such timber
transport that timber or lumber made from it

1853.plain: It is a federal crime to unlawfully cut, or recklessly injure or destroy, any tree on U.S. land reserved for public use, on an Indian reservation or tribal land, or on certain Indian allotments held in trust by the government.
keyPoints: Cutting must be unlawful, or injury must be wanton (reckless)
Covers reserved federal land, Indian reservations, and trust allotments
1853.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: unlawfully cuts, or wantonly injures or destroys any tree growing, standing, or being upon any land of the United States

act: cut, or recklessly injure or destroy, any tree on U.S. land

1854.plain: It is a federal crime to cut, chip, or box trees on U.S. lands (or lands under a pending federal land claim) to get pitch, turpentine, or similar substances. It is also a crime to buy or acquire such substances, or products made from them, knowing they were taken this way.
keyPoints: Cutting must be done to obtain pitch, turpentine, or similar substances
Buyers must know the materials were unlawfully obtained
1854.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: cuts, chips, chops, or boxes any tree upon any lands belonging to the United States
buys, trades for, or in any manner acquires any pitch, turpentine, or other substance

act: cut, chip, or box trees on U.S. lands
buy or acquire such substances
intent: to get pitch, turpentine, or similar substances

1855.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully set fire, without permission, to timber, brush, grass, or other burnable material on federal lands, Indian reservations, tribal lands, or certain Indian allotments.
keyPoints: Must be done willfully and without authority
Does not apply to an allottee reasonably using their own allotment
1855.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: sets on fire any timber, underbrush, or grass or other inflammable material upon the public domain

act: set fire, without permission, to timber, brush, grass, or other burnable material

1856.plain: It is a federal crime for a person who starts a fire in or near a forest or other burnable material on federal or Indian lands to leave it without fully putting it out, let it spread out of control, or leave it burning unattended.
keyPoints: Applies to the person who started or caused the fire
Covers federal lands, Indian reservations, tribal lands, and trust allotments
1856.penalty: Up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both
acts: leaves said fire without totally extinguishing the same
permits or suffers said fire to burn or spread beyond his control
leaves or suffers said fire to burn unattended

act: leave it without fully putting it out, let it spread out of control, or leave it burning unattended

1857.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly and unlawfully break or destroy a gate, fence, hedge, or wall around U.S. land reserved for public use. It is also a crime to drive livestock onto such land to destroy grass or trees (or where they may destroy them), or to knowingly let livestock enter through the fence where they can damage grass, trees, or other U.S. property.
keyPoints: Fence damage must be knowing and unlawful
Does not apply to unreserved public lands
1857.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: breaks, opens, or destroys any gate, fence, hedge, or wall inclosing any lands of the United States
drives any cattle, horses, hogs, or other livestock upon any such lands for the purposes of destroying the grass or trees
permits his cattle, horses, hogs, or other livestock to enter through any such inclosure upon any such lands of the United States

act: break or destroy a gate, fence, hedge, or wall
drive livestock onto such land
let livestock enter through the fence

1858.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully destroy, deface, change, or move government land survey markers, such as corner posts, marked witness trees, monuments, or bench marks.
keyPoints: Must be done willfully
Covers markers of any government survey
1858.penalty: Up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both
acts: destroys, defaces, changes, or removes to another place any section corner, quarter-section corner, or meander post
cuts down any witness tree or any tree blazed to mark the line of a Government survey
defaces, changes, or removes any monument or bench mark of any Government survey

act: destroy, deface, change, or move government land survey markers

1859.plain: It is a federal crime to use threats or force to interrupt, hinder, or stop authorized surveyors from surveying public lands or confirmed private land claims.
keyPoints: Must involve threats or force
Surveyors must be authorized under Bureau of Land Management instructions
1859.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: by threats or force, interrupts, hinders, or prevents the surveying of the public lands

act: use threats or force to interrupt, hinder, or stop authorized surveyors

1860.plain: It is a federal crime to make or try to make a deal with someone so they will not bid on U.S. land offered at public sale. It is also a crime to use intimidation, collusion, or unfair tactics to stop or try to stop anyone from bidding on such land.
keyPoints: Attempts are also covered
Applies to U.S. land offered at public sale
1860.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine of up to $1,000, or both
acts: bargains, contracts, or agrees, or attempts to bargain, contract, or agree with another that such other shall not bid upon or purchase any parcel of lands of the United States
by intimidation, combination, or unfair management, hinders, prevents, or attempts to hinder or prevent, any person from bidding upon or purchasing any tract of land

act: make or try to make a deal with someone so they will not bid on U.S. land
use intimidation, collusion, or unfair tactics to stop or try to stop anyone from bidding

1861.plain: It is a federal crime for a paid land locator to falsely tell a would-be buyer or settler that land is available U.S. public land, or that it has a certain surveyed description. This applies whether the lie is told on purpose to deceive or with reckless disregard for the truth and actually deceives the person.
keyPoints: Applies to people paid or promised pay to locate land
Must be willful intent to deceive, or reckless falsehood that deceives
1861.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both
acts: undertakes to locate for an intending purchaser, settler, or entryman any public lands of the United States
falsely represents to such intending purchaser, settler, or entryman that any tract of land shown to him is public land of the United States
falsely represents to any such person that any tract of land shown to him is public land of the United States

act: falsely tell a would-be buyer or settler that land is available U.S. public land
intent: with reckless disregard for the truth

1863.plain: It is a federal crime to go onto national forest land without permission while it is lawfully closed to the public by the Secretary of Agriculture.
keyPoints: Land must be closed under a lawful regulation
Applies only without lawful authority or permission
1863.penalty: Up to 6 months in prison, a fine, or both
acts: goes upon any national-forest land while it is closed to the public

act: go onto national forest land without permission while it is lawfully closed

1864.plain: It is a federal crime to place a hazardous device, such as a booby trap, trip-wire gun, or tree spike, on federal land or Indian land. This applies if done to break drug laws, to obstruct timber harvesting, or with reckless disregard for the risk of death or injury to others. Injured people may also sue the offender in civil court.
keyPoints: Must intend a drug crime or to obstruct logging, or act with extreme recklessness
Punishment increases if property damage, injury, or death results
Repeat offenders face up to 20 years even if no harm results
1864.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison or a fine; up to 20 years if property damage or over $10,000 in avoidance costs, injury, or a repeat offense; up to 40 years for serious injury; up to life if someone dies
acts: uses a hazardous or injurious device on Federal land, on an Indian reservation, or on an Indian allotment

act: place a hazardous device, such as a booby trap, trip-wire gun, or tree spike
intent: to break drug laws, to obstruct timber harvesting

1901.plain: It is a federal crime for a U.S. officer who collects or pays out government revenue to run a trade or business in federal or state funds, debts, or public property.
keyPoints: Applies only to officers handling collection or payment of U.S. revenue
Offender must be removed from office and barred from future federal office
1901.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both; removal from office and a ban on holding federal office

1902.plain: It is a federal crime for a government employee or agent to willfully leak confidential crop information that could affect market prices before its official release time. It is also a crime for them to trade in those crops before the information is made public.
keyPoints: Information must be required by law or rule to be withheld until a set time
Leak must be willful
Person must have actually known the rules they broke
1902.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both

Covers commodities, related contracts, and related company stock

1905.plain: It is a federal crime for a federal employee, or certain others working for the government, to disclose without legal authority confidential business or financial information they learned on the job. This includes trade secrets, income, and profits of people or companies, and also letting anyone see tax returns when the law does not allow it.

Information must come from official duties, investigations, or filed records

1905.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both; removal from office or job

1906.plain: It is a federal crime for a bank examiner, or a GAO employee with access to bank examination reports, to reveal borrower names or loan collateral of covered banks to anyone other than the bank's proper officers without written permission.

Exceptions for court orders, Congress, and authorized GAO uses
1906.penalty: Up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both

1907.plain: It is a federal crime for a farm credit examiner or other examiner to reveal borrower names of federal land banks or similar farm lending institutions to anyone other than their proper officers without written permission.

Exceptions for court orders and Congress
Offender is barred from serving as a farm credit examiner

1909.plain: It is a federal crime for a national bank examiner, FDIC examiner, or farm credit examiner to do any paid work for a bank, loan association, or anyone connected to one.
keyPoints: Applies only to these types of examiners
The other work must be for pay

1910.plain: It is a federal crime for a federal judge to appoint a close relative (by blood or marriage, up to the fourth degree) as a receiver or trustee (a person put in charge of property in a court case).
keyPoints: Applies to federal judges
Relative must be within the fourth degree by blood or marriage

1911.plain: It is a federal crime for a receiver, trustee, or manager holding property in a federal court case to willfully fail to manage it according to the state's laws, the same way an owner would have to.

Applies to property held in a pending federal court case

1912.plain: It is a federal crime for a federal officer, employee, or agent who inspects vessels to accept any fee or reward for that work beyond what the law allows.
keyPoints: Applies to federal vessel inspectors
Offender must forfeit their office

1913.plain: This section bars using money Congress has appropriated to lobby members of Congress or other officials on legislation or policy, unless Congress expressly allows it. Officials may still make requests through proper channels. Violations are treated as violations of 31 U.S.C. 1352(a).

1915.plain: It is a federal crime for a U.S. officer, without legal authority, to settle, reduce, or try to settle or reduce a government claim under customs laws, or to release anyone or anything from a customs fine, penalty, or forfeiture.

1916.plain: It is a federal crime to violate the rule that civil service workers in Washington, D.C. Executive departments may be employed only for work tied to the funding that pays them. 1917.plain: It is a federal crime for Office of Personnel Management staff or other public servants to willfully and corruptly interfere with civil service exams. This includes blocking someone's right to take an exam, falsifying grades, lying about results, or giving secret information to help or hurt a candidate.
keyPoints: Must be willful and corrupt

Each violation is a separate offense

1918.plain: It is a federal crime to hold or accept a federal or D.C. government job while advocating the overthrow of the constitutional government, or knowingly belonging to a group that does. It is also a crime to strike, claim a right to strike, or knowingly belong to an employee group claiming a right to strike against these governments.
keyPoints: Applies to holding or accepting federal or D.C. government jobs

1919.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly lie about, or knowingly hide, an important fact to get or increase unemployment payments for federal service, for oneself or someone else.

Covers payments under chapter 85 of title 5

1951.plain: It is a federal crime to obstruct, delay, or affect commerce by robbery or extortion (getting property through force, threats, fear, or abuse of official power), or to try or conspire (agree with others) to do so. It is also a crime to commit or threaten violence against a person or property as part of a plan to do any of this.

Attempts and conspiracies are covered

1952.plain: It is a federal crime to travel between states or countries, or use the mail or other interstate facilities, intending to spread profits from, promote, or carry on illegal activity, or to commit violence to help it, and then to do or attempt such an act. Illegal activity here includes gambling, drug, prostitution, or untaxed liquor businesses, plus extortion, bribery, arson, and money laundering.

Higher penalty for crimes of violence, highest if death results
Bank and credit union savings raffles are excluded

1954.plain: It is a federal crime for people who run or work for an employee benefit or pension plan, or for the employers, unions, or service providers connected to it, to ask for or take kickbacks, gifts, loans, or money in exchange for being influenced on plan matters. 1955.plain: It is a federal crime to run, pay for, manage, or own any part of an illegal gambling business. The business counts only if it breaks State or local law, involves five or more people, and either runs for more than 30 days or takes in $2,000 in a single day. Money and property used in the business can be taken by the government.
keyPoints: Gambling must be illegal under the State or local law where it happens
Five or more people must be involved in running it
Must run over 30 days or earn $2,000 in one day
Charity bingo or raffles by tax-exempt groups and savings promotion raffles are excluded

1956.plain: It is a federal crime to launder money, meaning to knowingly handle money from certain crimes in order to hide where it came from, to help more crime happen, to dodge taxes, or to avoid reporting rules. It is also a crime to move money into or out of the United States for these purposes, or to handle money that undercover agents say is dirty for these purposes. Conspiring to launder money is punished the same as the crime itself.
keyPoints: Must know the money came from some kind of felony
Purpose must be to hide the money, promote crime, evade taxes, or avoid reporting
Attempts and conspiracies are also covered
Violators can also face a civil penalty of the money's value or $10,000

1957.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly make a bank deposit, withdrawal, transfer, or similar money transaction of more than $10,000 using money that came from certain crimes. It applies to conduct in the United States, and to U.S. persons abroad. Payments needed to hire a criminal defense lawyer are not covered.

Government need not prove the person knew which specific crime
Attempts are also covered

1958.plain: It is a federal crime to travel between states or countries, or use the mail, phones, or other interstate services (or make someone else do so), intending that a murder be committed for pay. It covers both the person paying and the person being paid, and also anyone who conspires to do so.

Penalty rises if someone is injured or killed

1959.plain: It is a federal crime to murder, kidnap, maim, assault with a dangerous weapon or cause serious injury, or threaten violence against someone in exchange for payment from a criminal enterprise (an organized group involved in racketeering), or to join, stay in, or move up in such a group. 1962.plain: This is the main RICO law. 1963.plain: This section sets the punishment for RICO crimes under section 1962: up to 20 years in prison (or life if the underlying crime allows life) and a fine, plus forfeiture (the government taking) of property and profits tied to the crime. It also lays out the court procedures for freezing, seizing, and selling that property and for third parties to claim an interest in it.

1964.plain: This section lets federal courts stop RICO violations, for example by ordering a business broken up, and lets the Attorney General bring such cases. It also lets people whose business or property was harmed by a RICO violation sue for three times their damages plus legal costs.

1965.plain: This section says where civil racketeering (RICO) cases can be filed and how court papers and subpoenas (orders to appear) can be delivered to people in other districts.

1966.plain: In a civil racketeering case brought by the United States, the Attorney General can certify that the case is of general public importance, and a judge must then be assigned to hear it right away.

1967.plain: In civil racketeering cases brought by the United States, the court may decide whether the proceedings are open or closed to the public, after considering the rights of the people affected.

1968.plain: This section lets the Attorney General demand documents from people or businesses during a racketeering investigation, before any case is filed. It sets rules for what the demand must say, how it is delivered, how the documents are kept and returned, and how people can challenge the demand in court.

1991.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully and maliciously trespass on or enter a train, rail car, or locomotive intending to commit murder, robbery, violence against passengers or crew, or another crime against people or property on board. This applies in U.S. territories, districts, and places under exclusive federal jurisdiction.
keyPoints: Must be done willfully and maliciously
Intent to commit murder or robbery carries the higher penalty
Prosecutors need not prove a specific intended victim
1991.penalty: Up to 20 years in prison and/or a fine if the intent was murder or robbery; otherwise up to 1 year and/or a fine

1992.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly attack, wreck, derail, set fire to, or disable trains, mass transit vehicles, or their tracks, stations, signals, and other facilities. It also covers placing bombs, toxins, or hazardous materials near them, interfering with operators, attacking people on that property, scouting targets to plan an attack, giving false information about an attack, and attempts, threats, or conspiracies. The conduct must affect a railroad or mass transit provider, or involve crossing state lines.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly and without lawful authority
Harsher penalties if passengers, nuclear waste, or certain hazardous materials were on board
Death of any person raises the penalty to up to life or death (not for scouting, false information, or attempts/threats/conspiracies)
1992.penalty: Up to 20 years in prison and/or a fine; up to life if passengers or dangerous cargo were aboard; any term up to life, or death, if someone is killed

2251.plain: It is a federal crime to use, persuade, or force a minor into sexually explicit conduct, or transport a minor for that purpose, to make photos, videos, or live streams of it, when there is a link to interstate or foreign commerce, the mail, or materials moved across state lines. It is also a crime for parents or guardians to knowingly allow this, to do it abroad intending to bring the images into the U.S., or to knowingly post ads seeking or offering such material.

Applies to parents and guardians who permit the conduct
Prior sex-crime convictions sharply raise the minimum and maximum terms
Death or 30 years to life if someone dies

2251A.plain: It is a federal crime for a parent, guardian, or caretaker to sell or transfer custody of a child, or for anyone to buy or obtain custody of a child, knowing or intending that the child will be used in sexually explicit images. There must be a link to interstate or foreign travel or communication, or the conduct must occur in a U.S. territory.
keyPoints: Must act with knowledge or intent that the child will appear in sexually explicit images
Offers to sell or buy are also covered
Requires interstate/foreign travel or communication, or a U.S. territory
2251A.penalty: At least 30 years and up to life in prison, plus a fine

2252A.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly mail, transport, receive, distribute, sell, advertise, possess, or access with intent to view child pornography, when linked to interstate commerce, the mail, or federal land. It is also a crime to send sexual images to a minor to lure them into illegal activity, to make or share altered images of a real identifiable minor, or to run a child exploitation enterprise.

Defenses include proof all people shown were adults or no real minor was used
Victims may sue for damages
Child exploitation enterprise: repeated offenses with multiple victims, working with 3+ others

2252B.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly use a misleading website domain name to trick someone into viewing obscene material. Penalties are higher when the goal is to trick a minor into viewing material harmful to minors.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly with intent to deceive
Domain names with words like "sex" or "porn" are not misleading
Higher penalty when a minor is the target

2252C.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly put words or images in a website's source code (the underlying code of a web page) to trick someone into viewing obscene material. Penalties are higher when the goal is to trick a minor into viewing material harmful to minors.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly with intent to deceive
Words clearly showing sexual content, like "sex" or "porn", are not misleading
Higher penalty when a minor is the target

2253.plain: This section requires people convicted of certain child exploitation or federal sexual abuse crimes to give up (forfeit) the illegal images, any profits from the crime, and any property used to commit it. It follows the forfeiture procedures of the Controlled Substances Act.

2254.plain: This section allows the government to take property linked to child exploitation crimes through a civil (non-criminal) court case, using the procedures in chapter 46.

2255.plain: This section lets people who were victims of certain child sex crimes as minors sue the offender in federal court for actual damages or $150,000, plus legal costs and possibly punitive damages. There is no time limit for filing the lawsuit.

2257.plain: Anyone who produces books, films, photos, digital images, websites, or similar material showing real (not faked) sexually explicit conduct must check each performer's ID and keep records of their name, date of birth, and any other names they have used. The material must carry a notice saying where those records are kept. It is a federal crime to fail to keep these records, to make false entries, to leave off the notice, to refuse a government inspection, or to knowingly sell or transfer covered material that lacks the notice.
keyPoints: Applies to producers of material showing actual sexually explicit conduct
False entries and missing notices must be done knowingly
Sellers do not have to check whether the records or notice are accurate
Mere distribution, film processing, and internet hosting do not count as producing
2257.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison and/or a fine; 2 to 10 years for a repeat offender

It is a federal crime to fail to keep these records, make false entries, leave off the notice, refuse a government inspection, or knowingly sell covered material without the notice. Some commercial producers who certify to the Attorney General that they already keep performer records are exempt, but never for material that is child pornography.

2258.plain: It is a federal crime for certain professionals working on federal land or in a federally run or contracted facility, and other people covered by federal child abuse reporting law, to fail to report suspected child abuse on time. This applies when they learn facts that give reason to suspect a child has been abused. The specific people covered and the reporting rules are set by section 226 of the Victims of Child Abuse Act of 1990.
keyPoints: Applies to listed professionals on federal land or in federal facilities, and other covered individuals
Triggered by facts giving reason to suspect child abuse
Failing to make a timely report is the crime

2258A.plain: Online service providers must report to the CyberTipline of the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) as soon as reasonably possible after they actually learn of apparent child pornography, child sex trafficking, or online enticement of a child. A provider that knowingly and willfully fails to make a required report can be fined. The section also explains what a report may contain, who NCMEC sends reports to, limits on sharing the information, and how long providers must preserve reported material.
keyPoints: Applies to online service providers with actual knowledge of apparent violations
Failure to report must be knowing and willful
Providers are not required to monitor users or scan content
Fines are larger for providers with 100 million or more monthly users
2258A.penalty: Fines only: first failure up to $850,000 (100 million+ monthly users) or $600,000 (smaller providers); later failures up to $1,000,000 or $850,000

2258B.plain: This section protects online providers, domain name registrars, NCMEC's contracted vendors, and child pornography victims (or their representatives) from being sued or charged for reporting or storing apparent child pornography as part of reporting it to NCMEC. The protection does not apply to intentional misconduct, actual malice, or reckless behavior, and it requires them to limit access to and destroy such images when asked.

2258C.plain: This section lets NCMEC share technical details from CyberTipline reports, such as hash values (digital fingerprints of images), with online providers and law enforcement to help stop child pornography. It limits how those details may be used and does not allow sharing the actual images with providers.

2258D.plain: This section protects NCMEC and its staff from being sued or charged for carrying out its CyberTipline work and efforts to identify child victims. The protection does not cover intentional misconduct, malice, recklessness, or ordinary business activities, and NCMEC must limit access to and destroy images when law enforcement asks.

2259.plain: Courts must order people convicted of child sexual exploitation crimes in this chapter to pay restitution (money to repay victims for their losses), and in child pornography trafficking cases at least $3,000 per victim. Victims of child pornography trafficking may also choose a one-time payment from a federal victims fund. It is a federal crime for a lawyer helping a victim get that payment to charge fees and costs above 15 percent of it.
keyPoints: Restitution is mandatory and cannot be reduced for the defendant's finances
Attorney fees for fund payments are capped at 15 percent
The crime applies to attorneys who exceed the fee cap
2259.penalty: For attorneys who overcharge: up to 1 year in prison and/or a fine

2259A.plain: This section requires courts to add a special money charge, called an assessment, on people convicted of child pornography crimes: up to $17,000 for possession-type offenses, up to $35,000 for other trafficking offenses, and up to $50,000 for production offenses. These amounts are adjusted each year for inflation, and the section sets the order in which a defendant's payments are applied.

2259B.plain: This section sets up how the Child Pornography Victims Reserve, a federal fund, is filled and used. Money from child pornography assessments and private donations goes into the fund, which pays victims the one-time assistance allowed under section 2259, earliest orders first.

2260.plain: It is a federal crime for someone outside the United States to use, persuade, or force a minor into sexually explicit conduct, or transport a minor for that purpose, to make images or live video, intending them to be sent into the United States or its nearby waters. It is also a crime for someone outside the United States to knowingly receive, ship, sell, distribute, or possess to ship or sell such images of a minor, intending them to be brought into the United States. Attempts and conspiracies are covered too.
keyPoints: Conduct happens outside the United States
Must intend the images to enter the U.S. or waters within 12 miles of its coast
Distribution offenses must be done knowingly

2260A.plain: This section adds a mandatory extra 10 years in prison for anyone required to register as a sex offender who commits certain felony crimes involving a minor, such as kidnapping, sexual abuse, child sex trafficking, or child pornography production. The extra 10 years must be served after the sentence for the underlying crime, not at the same time.

2261.plain: It is a federal crime to travel across state or national lines, or into or out of Indian country or federal territory, intending to kill, injure, harass, or intimidate a spouse, intimate partner, or dating partner, and then commit or attempt a violent crime against that person. It is also a crime to force or trick a partner into traveling across those lines and commit or attempt a violent crime against them.

Victim must be a spouse, intimate partner, or dating partner
Penalty increases with the victim's injuries or use of a dangerous weapon
At least 1 year in prison for stalking in violation of a protective order

2261A.plain: It is a federal crime to stalk someone. This covers traveling across state or national lines, into or out of Indian country, or being on federal land or waters, intending to kill, injure, harass, intimidate, or spy on someone. It also covers using the mail, the internet, phones, or other interstate services to carry out a pattern of such conduct.

Conduct must cause reasonable fear of death or serious injury, or substantial emotional distress
Protects the victim, family members, spouses or partners, and their pets or service animals

2262.plain: It is a federal crime to cross state or national lines, enter or leave Indian country, or be on federal land or waters, intending to violate a protection order (a court order keeping someone away from another person), and then violate it. It is also a crime to force or trick a person into traveling and then violate a protection order protecting them.
keyPoints: Applies to parts of an order banning violence, threats, harassment, contact, or coming near someone
Also protects the person's pet, service animal, emotional support animal, or horse
Penalty rises with injury, weapon use, or death of the victim
If conduct is a sexual abuse crime, penalty follows chapter 109A
2262.penalty: A fine and/or up to 5 years in prison; up to 10 years for serious injury or use of a dangerous weapon; up to 20 years for permanent disfigurement or life-threatening injury; up to life if the victim dies; sex-abuse offenses punished as under chapter 109A

2263.plain: When a court decides whether someone charged with domestic violence or stalking crimes can be released before trial, the alleged victim must be given a chance to speak about the danger the defendant poses.

2264.plain: This section requires courts to order restitution (repayment to the victim) for any domestic violence or stalking crime in this chapter. The defendant must pay the full amount of the victim's losses, such as medical care, therapy, housing, lost income, legal fees, and vet bills, no matter the defendant's finances or the victim's insurance.

2265.plain: This section requires every State, tribe, and territory to honor and enforce valid protection orders issued by courts in other States, tribes, or territories. It also limits notifying the abuser of registration and bars posting information online that could reveal where a protected person is.

2265A.plain: This section doubles the maximum prison term for a domestic violence or stalking crime in this chapter if the offender already has a prior conviction for domestic violence or stalking under federal, State, or tribal law.

2271.plain: It is a federal crime to conspire (agree with someone) to sink or destroy a ship in order to cheat its insurers or lenders. It is also a crime to build or equip a ship within the United States for that purpose.

Must intend to harm insurers of the ship or cargo, or lenders on the ship
Applies on the high seas or within the United States

Must intend to harm insurers, cargo owners, or co-owners
Applies only to an owner or part owner

It is also a crime to knowingly let the ship be used by people planning crimes against the United States, to cheat the United States, or in violation of U.S. treaty or international law duties.

A ship knowingly misused can be seized and forfeited (taken by the government)

2275.plain: It is a federal crime to set fire to certain ships or their cargo, tamper with their engines or navigation equipment, plant bombs or explosives on them, or do anything else to them meant to damage or endanger the ship, cargo, or people aboard. It covers foreign and U.S. ships in U.S. jurisdiction, and U.S. ships on the high seas.

Covers harm meant to happen after the ship leaves U.S. waters
Attempts are covered

It is also a crime to maliciously cut or destroy ropes, cables, or buoys attached to a ship's anchor or moorings. This applies on the high seas or other U.S. maritime waters outside any State's jurisdiction.

2277.plain: It is a federal crime to bring, carry, or have a dangerous weapon or explosive on board a U.S.-documented ship, or a ship taken over by the United States, without permission from the owner or captain. For ships under U.S. government control or guard, permission must come from the captain of the port.
keyPoints: Applies only without prior permission
Does not apply to military personnel or authorized government officers on duty

2278.plain: It is a federal crime for the captain of certain passenger ships to carry explosives, gunpowder, strong acids, or other cargo likely to endanger passengers or the ship. Explosives or gunpowder for the ship's own use are allowed.

Exception for items for the ship's own use
Exception where the law expressly allows it

2279.plain: It is a federal crime to board a ship that is about to arrive at its destination before it has arrived and been fully tied up, unless the person is in U.S. government service or authorized by law. The ship's captain may hold the person and turn them over to police.
keyPoints: Exception for U.S. service members and people authorized by law
Applies before the ship is completely moored
2279.penalty: A fine, up to 6 months in prison, or both

2280.plain: It is a federal crime to hijack a ship, commit violence on board that endangers its navigation, damage or plant a device on a ship, wreck navigation facilities, or give false information that endangers a ship. Injuring or killing someone in the process, and attempts or conspiracies, are also covered. Threatening some of these acts is a separate crime.

Does not apply to armed forces in armed conflict or military forces on official duty
No federal case for U.S. labor-dispute conduct that is a State felony

2280a.plain: It is a federal crime to use a ship to carry out terror attacks, such as using or releasing explosives, nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons, or hazardous substances like oil, to frighten a population or pressure a government. It is also a crime to transport such weapons or related materials on a ship, or to transport an offender to help them escape prosecution. Injuring or killing someone in the process, threats, attempts, and conspiracies are also covered.

2281.plain: It is a federal crime to seize an offshore fixed platform (such as an oil rig) by force or threats, commit violence on it, damage it, or place a device on it in a way that endangers its safety. Injuring or killing someone in the process, and attempts or conspiracies, are also covered. Threatening some of these acts is a separate crime.
keyPoints: Must act unlawfully and intentionally
Acts must be likely to endanger the platform's safety
Does not apply to armed forces in armed conflict or military forces on official duty
No federal case for U.S. labor-dispute conduct that is a State felony
2281.penalty: A fine and up to 20 years in prison; death or up to life if someone dies; threats: up to 5 years and a fine

2281a.plain: It is a federal crime to use or release explosives, radioactive material, or biological, chemical, or nuclear weapons on or from an offshore fixed platform (such as an oil rig), or to discharge oil or other dangerous substances from one, to frighten a population or pressure a government. Injuring or killing someone in the process, attempts, conspiracies, and threats are also covered.
keyPoints: Must act unlawfully and intentionally
Purpose must be to intimidate a population or coerce a government or international organization
Act must cause or be likely to cause death or serious injury or damage
Exceptions for armed forces in armed conflict and military on official duty
2281a.penalty: A fine and up to 20 years in prison; up to life if someone dies; threats: up to 5 years and a fine

2282B.plain: It is a federal crime to intentionally destroy, seriously damage, change, move, or tamper with official aids to ship navigation, such as buoys and markers maintained by the Coast Guard or the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation.
keyPoints: Must be done intentionally
Act must endanger or be likely to endanger safe navigation of a ship
2282B.penalty: A fine, up to 20 years in prison, or both

act: destroy, seriously damage, change, move, or tamper with official aids to ship navigation

2283.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly carry an explosive or fire-starting device, biological agent, chemical weapon, or radioactive or nuclear material on a ship, knowing it is meant to be used to commit a federal terrorism crime. This applies to ships in U.S. waters, on the high seas, or with U.S. nationality.
keyPoints: Must know the transport is happening
Must know the item is intended for a listed terrorism offense
Death penalty possible if the conduct causes someone's death
2283.penalty: A fine and/or prison for any term up to life; death is possible if someone is killed

2284.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly and intentionally carry a terrorist on a ship, knowing the person is a terrorist. A terrorist here means someone who plans to commit, or is fleeing after committing, a listed federal terrorism crime. This applies to ships in U.S. waters, on the high seas, or with U.S. nationality.
keyPoints: Must act knowingly and intentionally
Must know the passenger is a terrorist
2284.penalty: A fine and/or prison for any term up to life
acts: transports any terrorist aboard any vessel

act: carry a terrorist on a ship

2285.plain: It is a federal crime to operate, try or plan to operate, or ride in a submarine-type or semi-submarine vessel that has no nationality (is not registered to any country) in international waters, with the intent to avoid detection. The crime can be prosecuted even if it happens outside the United States.
keyPoints: Must act knowingly and intend to evade detection
Certain signs of hiding can be treated as evidence of that intent
Defenses: vessel was lawfully registered, properly classed, lawfully operated, or using tracking systems
Does not apply to authorized U.S. government activities
2285.penalty: A fine, up to 15 years in prison, or both
acts: operates, or attempts or conspires to operate, by any means, or embarks in any submersible vessel or semi-submersible vessel that is without nationality

Must act knowingly and intend to evade detection

2290.plain: This section says when federal courts have power over the crimes in this chapter on destroying or interfering with ships and maritime facilities, including some crimes committed outside the United States involving U.S. citizens or U.S. vessels. It also says the chapter does not apply to lawful activities of the U.S. government.

2291.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly set fire to, damage, destroy, or disable a ship or boat, or to plant a bomb or explosive on or near one. It is also a crime to damage or violently interfere with port and navigation facilities (such as locks, canals, and navigation aids) or equipment used to load, store, or run ships, to attack people on a ship in a way that endangers it or seriously injure people at such facilities, or to give false information that endangers a ship. Attempts, conspiracies, and threats to do these things are also crimes.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Does not cover lawful activity such as normal repair, salvage, or approved hazardous-material shipping
Up to life if the ship carried high-level radioactive waste or spent nuclear fuel
Death penalty possible if the person intended to kill and someone died
2291.penalty: Up to 20 years in prison and a fine; up to life if the ship carried nuclear waste or spent nuclear fuel; death or up to life if someone is killed and death was intended; threats: up to 5 years, a fine, and the costs caused by the threat

2292.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly, maliciously, or with reckless disregard for human life spread false information about an attempt to attack a ship or maritime facility or to commit another federal shipping crime. Giving such false information knowing it is false, even without malice, can lead to a civil fine (a money penalty in a non-criminal case).
keyPoints: The person must know the information is false
Criminal penalty requires knowing, intentional, malicious, or reckless conduct
Covers false reports about crimes against ships, maritime facilities, or shipping
2292.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison or a fine; otherwise a civil penalty of up to $5,000

2293.plain: This section blocks federal prosecution under this chapter for certain conduct that is already a State crime, such as conduct tied to a labor dispute that is a State felony, or conduct that is only a State misdemeanor.

2312.plain: It is a federal crime to move a stolen car, boat, or aircraft across state lines or national borders while knowing it was stolen.
keyPoints: The person must know the vehicle was stolen
Covers motor vehicles, boats, and aircraft
The vehicle must be moved between states or countries
2312.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison and a fine

2313.plain: It is a federal crime to receive, keep, hide, store, trade, or sell a stolen car, boat, or aircraft that has crossed a state or U.S. border after being stolen, if the person knows it was stolen.
keyPoints: The person must know the vehicle was stolen
The vehicle must have crossed a state or national border after the theft
Covers motor vehicles, boats, and aircraft

2314.plain: It is a federal crime to move stolen or fraud-obtained goods, securities, or money worth $5,000 or more across state or national lines, knowing they were stolen. It is also a crime to bring fraud victims across state lines as part of a scheme to cheat them out of $5,000 or more, or to transport forged securities, forged tax stamps, forged traveler's checks, or tools for counterfeiting. Moving stolen veterans' memorials (such as grave markers or headstones) across state lines is also covered.
keyPoints: Must know the items were stolen, or act with fraudulent intent
Most property must be worth $5,000 or more
Does not apply to counterfeit U.S. or foreign government money and securities
Stolen veterans' memorial objects worth under $1,000 carry a lower penalty
2314.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison and a fine; up to 1 year if veterans' memorial objects are worth under $1,000; if a pre-retail medical product is involved, the penalty under section 670 applies if higher

2315.plain: It is a federal crime to receive, keep, hide, store, trade, or sell stolen goods, securities, or money worth $5,000 or more that have crossed a state or U.S. border, knowing they were stolen. It is also a crime to pledge or accept such stolen property worth $500 or more as security for a loan, to deal in forged securities or tax stamps or counterfeiting tools, or to deal in stolen veterans' memorials that crossed state lines.
keyPoints: Must know the property was stolen or forged
Value threshold is $5,000, or $500 when used as loan security
Does not apply to counterfeit U.S. or foreign government money and securities
Stolen veterans' memorial objects worth under $1,000 carry a lower penalty

2316.plain: It is a federal crime to move stolen livestock across state or national lines while knowing the animals were stolen.
keyPoints: The person must know the livestock was stolen
The livestock must be moved between states or countries
2316.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison and a fine

2317.plain: It is a federal crime to receive, hide, store, trade, buy, or sell stolen livestock that is moving in or part of trade between states or countries, while knowing it was stolen.
keyPoints: The person must know the livestock was stolen
The livestock must be part of interstate or foreign trade
2317.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison and a fine

2318.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly deal in fake labels, or real labels used without permission, for music, software, movies, books, artwork, or their packaging. It is also a crime to deal in fake documentation or packaging for these works. Copyright owners harmed by these acts can also sue for damages.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Covers fake labels and genuine labels misused without the copyright owner's permission
Applies when mail or interstate commerce is used, or copyrighted works are involved, among other situations
Victims may sue for $2,500 to $25,000 per violation instead of actual losses
2318.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison and a fine; forfeiture and restitution under section 2323

2319.plain: This section sets the criminal punishments for willful copyright infringement, which is defined in section 506(a) of title 17 (the copyright law). The punishment depends on how many copies were made or shared, their value, whether it was done for profit, and whether it was a repeat offense.
keyPoints: The crime itself is defined in section 506(a) of title 17
Higher penalties for 10 or more copies worth over $2,500
Higher penalties for commercial gain and for repeat felony offenses
Victims may submit impact statements before sentencing
2319.penalty: Up to 1, 3, 5, or 6 years in prison and a fine depending on the type and size of the infringement; up to 10 years for some repeat offenses

2319A.plain: It is a federal crime to record or broadcast a live music performance without the performers' consent, or to copy, sell, rent, or distribute such bootleg recordings, when done for profit. This applies even if the recording was made outside the United States.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly and for commercial advantage or financial gain
Performers did not consent
Bootleg copies made abroad can be seized at the border
2319A.penalty: Up to 5 years in prison and a fine; up to 10 years for a second or later offense

2319B.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly use, or try to use, a camera or other recording device to record or transmit a movie being shown in a theater without the copyright owner's permission. Theater owners and staff may briefly detain a suspect to question them or call police.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly and without permission
Just having a recording device in a theater is not enough for conviction
Authorized law-enforcement and intelligence activities are exempt
2319B.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison and a fine; up to 6 years for a second or later offense

2319C.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully run, for profit, an online streaming service that is mainly built to show copyrighted works without permission. This also covers services with no real use besides illegal streaming, or that are marketed for illegal streaming.
keyPoints: Must be willful and for commercial advantage or financial gain
Service must be mainly designed, used, or marketed for unauthorized streaming
Higher penalty for streaming works not yet commercially released
Higher penalty for repeat offenses
2319C.penalty: Up to 3 years in prison and a fine; up to 5 years for unreleased works; up to 10 years for a second or later offense

2320.plain: It is a federal crime to intentionally sell or deal in goods or services that carry a counterfeit (fake) trademark, or labels and packaging bearing one. Dealing in counterfeit military goods and counterfeit drugs is also a crime and is punished more harshly. Attempts and conspiracies are covered too.
keyPoints: Must be intentional, with knowledge the mark is counterfeit
Harsher penalties for counterfeit military goods, drugs, and repeat offenses
Up to life in prison if the person knowingly or recklessly causes death
Repackaging genuine goods without intent to deceive is not covered
2320.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison and a fine up to $2,000,000 for individuals ($5,000,000 for companies); up to 20 or 30 years and larger fines for repeat offenses, military goods, drugs, or serious injury; up to life if death results
