2321.plain: It is a federal crime to buy, receive, or keep a car or car part with plans to sell it, knowing its identification number (such as a VIN) has been removed or altered.
keyPoints: Must know the identification number was removed or altered
Must intend to sell or otherwise dispose of the vehicle or part
Does not apply if damage was caused by a collision or fire, or if the alteration was lawful under section 511
2321.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison and a fine
acts: buys, receives, possesses, or obtains control of, with intent to sell or otherwise dispose of, a motor vehicle or motor vehicle part

act: buy, receive, or keep a car or car part

2322.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly own, run, or work in a chop shop. A chop shop is a place where stolen cars or car parts are taken apart, disguised, or have their identification numbers changed so they can be sold across state or national lines.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Covers owners, operators, and people working in the chop shop
Maximum prison time and fine double for repeat convictions
The government may also seek a court order to shut down the operation
2322.penalty: Up to 15 years in prison and a fine; up to 30 years and double the fine for a repeat conviction
acts: owns, operates, maintains, or controls a chop shop or conducts operations in a chop shop

act: own, run, or work in a chop shop
penalty: Maximum prison time and fine double

2323.plain: This section allows the government to take and destroy counterfeit and pirated goods, along with property used to make them and profits from these crimes. It also requires people convicted of copyright and trademark counterfeiting crimes to repay their victims.

2326.plain: This section adds extra prison time for certain fraud and identity crimes defined elsewhere when they are committed through telemarketing or email marketing. The extra time is larger if the crime targeted people over 55 or harmed ten or more of them.

2327.plain: This section requires courts to order people convicted of telemarketing or email marketing fraud to repay victims the full amount of their losses. Courts cannot skip this because the defendant is poor or the victim has insurance.

2328.plain: This section requires people convicted of telemarketing or email marketing fraud to give up the money they made from the crime and any equipment or software used to commit it.

2332.plain: It is a federal crime to kill a U.S. national (a U.S. citizen or someone who owes permanent loyalty to the U.S.) while that person is outside the United States. It is also a crime, outside the U.S., to try or conspire to kill a U.S. national, or to use physical violence meant to cause, or that causes, serious bodily injury to one.
keyPoints: Victim must be a U.S. national; conduct or victim is outside the United States
Murder, voluntary manslaughter, and involuntary manslaughter carry different penalties
Conspiracy requires at least one overt act toward the killing
Prosecution needs the Attorney General's written certification that the act aimed to coerce, intimidate, or retaliate against a government or civilians
2332.penalty: Murder: death or any term up to life and a fine; voluntary manslaughter: up to 10 years; involuntary manslaughter: up to 3 years; attempted murder: up to 20 years; conspiracy to murder: up to life; serious violence: up to 10 years
acts: kills a national of the United States
attempts to kill, or engages in a conspiracy to kill, a national of the United States
engages in physical violence

act: kill a U.S. national
use physical violence
intent: meant to cause, or that causes, serious bodily injury

2332a.plain: It is a federal crime to use, threaten to use, or try or conspire to use a weapon of mass destruction without lawful authority. This covers attacks on U.S. nationals abroad, on people or property in the U.S. when interstate or foreign commerce is involved, on U.S. government property anywhere, and on foreign-government property in the U.S. It also covers any U.S. national who does this outside the United States.
keyPoints: Weapons of mass destruction include destructive devices, chemical, biological, and radiation weapons
Threats, attempts, and conspiracies are punished like actual use
Must be done without lawful authority
Death penalty possible if someone dies
2332a.penalty: Any number of years up to life in prison; if death results, death or up to life
acts: uses, threatens, or attempts or conspires to use, a weapon of mass destruction
uses, or threatens, attempts, or conspires to use, a weapon of mass destruction outside of the United States

act: use, threaten to use, or try or conspire to use a weapon of mass destruction

2332b.plain: It is a federal crime, as part of conduct that crosses national borders, to kill, kidnap, maim, seriously injure, or assault someone with a dangerous weapon in the United States, or to damage property in the U.S. in a way that creates a substantial risk of serious injury. Threats, attempts, and conspiracies to do these things are also crimes. A federal link is required, such as use of the mail, effect on commerce, a U.S. government victim or property, or U.S. waters.
keyPoints: Conduct must occur both outside and inside the United States
Act must also violate a State or federal law
Prosecutors need not prove the defendant knew of the federal link
No probation; prison term must run consecutively to any other sentence
2332b.penalty: Killing or death: death or up to life; kidnapping: up to life; maiming: up to 35 years; serious assault: up to 30 years; property damage: up to 25 years; threats: up to 10 years; attempts/conspiracies: same maximum as completed crime
acts: kills, kidnaps, maims, commits an assault resulting in serious bodily injury, or assaults with a dangerous weapon any person within the United States
creates a substantial risk of serious bodily injury to any other person by destroying or damaging any structure, conveyance, or other real or personal property within the United States
threatens to commit an offense under paragraph (1), or attempts or conspires to do so

act: kill, kidnap, maim
assault someone with a dangerous weapon
damage property in the U.S.

2332d.plain: It is a federal crime for a U.S. person (citizens, nationals, permanent residents, U.S. companies, or anyone in the U.S.) to do a financial transaction with the government of a country officially listed as supporting international terrorism. This applies when the person knows, or has reasonable cause to know, of the country's listing.
keyPoints: Must know or have reasonable cause to know the country is designated as supporting terrorism
Transaction must be with that country's government
Exceptions allowed by Treasury Department regulations
2332d.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both
acts: engages in a financial transaction with the government of that country

act: do a financial transaction with the government of a country

2332e.plain: This section lets the Attorney General ask the Secretary of Defense for military help in enforcing the weapons-of-mass-destruction law (section 2332a) during an emergency involving such a weapon.

2332f.plain: It is a federal crime to unlawfully deliver, place, or set off an explosive or other deadly device (such as chemical, biological, or radioactive) in or against a public place, a government facility, a public transportation system, or an infrastructure facility like water or energy systems. The intent must be to cause death or serious injury, or major destruction likely causing major economic loss. Attempts and conspiracies are also covered.
keyPoints: Must intend death, serious injury, or extensive destruction causing major economic loss
Requires an international link, such as a foreign victim, foreign perpetrator, or attack abroad on U.S. interests
Does not apply to armed forces in armed conflict or military forces on official duty
Excludes purely domestic cases with U.S. citizen offender and victims
2332f.penalty: Punished as provided in section 2332a(a): any term up to life in prison; death or up to life if death results
acts: delivers, places, discharges, or detonates an explosive or other lethal device in, into, or against a place of public use, a state or government facility, a public transportation system, or an infrastructure facility
attempts or conspires to commit an offense under paragraph (1)

act: deliver, place, or set off an explosive or other deadly device
intent: to cause death or serious injury

2332g.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly make, acquire, transfer, receive, possess, import, export, or use guided missiles or rockets designed to target aircraft, their launchers, or parts for them. Possessing such a weapon and threatening to use it is also a crime. Attempts and conspiracies are covered.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Does not apply to devices not designed as weapons
Exempts conduct by or under contract with U.S. or State governments
Higher minimum if the weapon is used or threatened; life if death results
2332g.penalty: Fine up to $2,000,000 and 25 years to life in prison; 30 years to life if the weapon is used or threatened; mandatory life if a death results
acts: produce, construct, otherwise acquire, transfer directly or indirectly, receive, possess, import, export, or use, or possess and threaten to use
violates, or attempts or conspires to violate, subsection (a)

act: make, acquire, transfer, receive, possess, import, export, or use guided missiles

2332h.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly make, acquire, transfer, receive, possess, import, export, or use a weapon or device designed to release dangerous radiation (often called a "dirty bomb"). Possessing one and threatening to use it is also a crime, as are attempts and conspiracies.
keyPoints: Must be done knowingly
Exempts conduct by or under contract with the U.S. government
Higher minimum if the device is used or threatened; life if death results
2332h.penalty: Fine up to $2,000,000 and 25 years to life in prison; 30 years to life if the device is used or threatened; mandatory life if a death results

2332i.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly and unlawfully possess radioactive material or a nuclear or radiation device with intent to cause death, serious injury, or major damage. It is also a crime to use such material or devices, or damage or interfere with a nuclear facility, to cause harm or to force a person, group, or country to act. Believable threats, demands for nuclear material by threat or force, attempts, and conspiracies are also crimes.

Requires intent to cause harm or coerce, or knowledge that harm is likely

2333.plain: This section lets U.S. nationals hurt by international terrorism, or their families or heirs, sue in federal court for three times their damages plus legal costs. It also allows suits against those who knowingly help or conspire with designated foreign terrorist organizations.

2334.plain: This section sets where civil lawsuits for terrorism injuries under section 2333 can be filed and limits dismissing them for an inconvenient location. It also treats certain payments or U.S. activities by the Palestinian Authority and Palestine Liberation Organization as consent to be sued in U.S. courts.

2335.plain: This section requires civil terrorism lawsuits under section 2333 to be filed within 10 years. Time when the defendant is out of the country or hiding does not count.

2336.plain: This section bars civil terrorism lawsuits for injuries caused by acts of war. It also lets the government pause evidence-gathering or the whole lawsuit if it would interfere with a criminal case or national security operation.

2337.plain: This section bars civil terrorism lawsuits under section 2333 against the U.S. government, foreign governments, or their officials acting in their official roles.

2338.plain: This section gives federal district courts the only power to hear lawsuits brought under this chapter.

2339.plain: It is a federal crime to hide or shelter someone you know, or have reasonable grounds to believe, has committed or is about to commit certain serious terrorism crimes. These include attacks on aircraft, biological, chemical, or nuclear weapons crimes, bombing government property, weapons of mass destruction, and aircraft hijacking.

Applies only to the listed terrorism offenses
Can be prosecuted where the underlying crime happened
2339.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both

2339A.plain: It is a federal crime to provide material support or resources (such as money, lodging, training, weapons, false documents, transportation, or people), or to hide its nature, location, source, or ownership, knowing or intending it will be used for certain terrorism crimes. Support meant to help hide an escape after such a crime is also covered, as are attempts and conspiracies.
keyPoints: Must know or intend that the support will be used for a listed terrorism crime
Medicine and religious materials are not considered material support
Life in prison possible if someone dies
2339A.penalty: Up to 15 years in prison, a fine, or both; any term up to life if death results

2339B.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly give material support or resources (such as money, weapons, training, expert help, or people) to a foreign terrorist organization, or to try or plan to do so. Banks and other financial institutions that find they hold money belonging to such a group must freeze it and report it to the Treasury Department. Banks that knowingly fail to do so face civil fines.

Attempts and conspiracies are also crimes

2339C.plain: It is a federal crime to willfully provide or collect money or other assets knowing or intending that they will be used for terrorist acts, such as acts meant to kill or seriously injure civilians to intimidate people or pressure a government. It is also a crime to knowingly hide the nature, source, location, ownership, or control of money or support meant for terrorists. The law covers many situations inside and outside the United States.

The money does not have to actually be used for an attack
Attempts and conspiracies are also crimes
Hiding terrorist funds or support is a separate crime

2339D.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly receive military-type training (such as training in weapons, explosives, or ways to kill people or damage infrastructure) from or for a designated foreign terrorist organization. The law reaches conduct inside or outside the United States, including by U.S. citizens, permanent residents, and people later found in the United States.

2340A.plain: It is a federal crime to commit or try to commit torture outside the United States. It applies to U.S. nationals and to anyone present in the United States, no matter the nationality of the victim or offender. Planning torture with others (conspiracy) is also a crime.

Offender must be a U.S. national or be present in the U.S.

2342.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly ship, transport, receive, possess, sell, distribute, or buy contraband cigarettes or smokeless tobacco. 2343.plain: This section requires people who ship, sell, or distribute large amounts of cigarettes or smokeless tobacco to keep records and, for mail-order or online sales, file monthly reports with the Attorney General and state officials. It also lets federal ATF officers inspect their records and tobacco during business hours, with a civil fine of up to $10,000 for refusing access.

2344.plain: This section sets the criminal penalties for the federal contraband tobacco laws. It is a crime to knowingly deal in contraband cigarettes or smokeless tobacco, to knowingly break rules issued under these laws, or to make false statements in those records. Contraband tobacco can be seized and must be destroyed rather than resold.

Breaking the chapter's rules or making false records carries a lower maximum

2345.plain: This section says the federal contraband tobacco law does not take away states' and local governments' power to make and enforce their own cigarette tax laws. It also allows states and localities to keep working together to enforce those laws.

2346.plain: This section puts the Attorney General in charge of enforcing the federal contraband tobacco law and allows the Attorney General to issue rules. It also lets states, local governments, and licensed tobacco businesses sue in federal court to stop violations, with limits on suits against Indian tribes.

2381.plain: It is a federal crime, called treason, for a person who owes loyalty to the United States to wage war against the country or to side with its enemies by giving them help, whether inside the U.S. or elsewhere.

Must wage war against the U.S. or give aid and comfort to its enemies

2382.plain: It is a federal crime for a person who owes loyalty to the United States to know that treason has been committed and hide it instead of reporting it promptly to the President, a federal judge, or a state governor or judge. This is called misprision (concealment) of treason.
keyPoints: Applies to people who owe allegiance to the United States

keyPoints: Covers starting, inciting, assisting, or joining an uprising
Giving aid or comfort to it is also covered
A person convicted can never hold federal office

2384.plain: It is a federal crime for two or more people to agree to use force to overthrow the U.S. government, wage war against it, oppose its authority, block the carrying out of federal law, or seize federal property. This is called seditious conspiracy.

2385.plain: It is a federal crime to knowingly or willfully urge or teach that any government in the United States should be overthrown by force, violence, or assassination. 2426.plain: This section increases punishment for repeat offenders: anyone convicted under this chapter after a prior sex offense conviction faces up to three times the usual maximum prison term (unless a separate mandatory life rule in section 3559(e) applies). 2441.plain: It is a federal crime to commit a war crime, inside or outside the United States, if the crime happens at least partly in the U.S., if the victim or offender is a U.S. national, permanent resident, or member of the U.S. military, or if the offender is later found in the U.S. War crimes include grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and certain other treaties, such as torture, cruel treatment, murder, maiming, rape, sexual assault, hostage-taking, and harmful biological experiments on people in one's custody.

2512.penalty: A fine, up to 5 years in prison, or both

manufactures, assembles, possesses, or sells any electronic, mechanical, or other device
places in any newspaper, magazine, handbill, or other publication or disseminates by electronic means any advertisement

act: mail, ship, make, assemble, possess, or sell a device
Advertising such devices

2513.plain: This section allows the government to seize and keep (forfeit) any eavesdropping device used, made, sold, or advertised illegally under sections 2511 or 2512. It applies the customs-law rules for seizure and forfeiture, carried out by officers the Attorney General chooses.

2515.plain: This section bars courts, grand juries, agencies, and legislatures from using the contents of illegally intercepted phone calls or conversations, or any evidence derived from them, if disclosing that information would violate this chapter.

2516.plain: This section lists who may ask a judge for permission to wiretap phone calls, conversations, or electronic messages, and for which crimes. Senior Justice Department officials may seek federal wiretaps for a long list of serious crimes, state prosecutors may seek them under state law for certain serious crimes, and any federal prosecutor may seek to intercept electronic messages for any federal felony.

2517.plain: This section says when law enforcement officers who lawfully intercepted phone calls, conversations, or electronic messages may share or use what they learned. It allows sharing with other officers and certain officials (including foreign and national security officials in some cases), use in official duties, and use as testimony in court, and it says privileged communications (such as lawyer-client talks) keep their protection.

2518.plain: This section sets out the step-by-step rules for getting a court order to wiretap or intercept communications, including what the application must show, how long an order can last (no more than 30 days at a time), emergency interceptions, sealing of records, notice to people who were monitored, and motions to throw out unlawfully intercepted evidence. Breaking its record-sealing rules can be punished as contempt of court (disobeying a court).

2519.plain: This section requires judges and prosecutors to file yearly reports about wiretap orders they applied for, granted, or denied, and the results. The courts' Administrative Office then sends a yearly summary report to Congress.

2520.plain: This section lets a person whose calls, conversations, or electronic messages were illegally intercepted, shared, or used sue the wrongdoer (other than the United States) for money damages, court orders, and lawyer's fees. It sets how damages are figured, gives a defense for good-faith reliance on a warrant or court order, and sets a two-year deadline to sue.

2521.plain: This section lets the Attorney General ask a federal court to stop (enjoin) someone who is committing or about to commit a felony violation of the federal wiretapping laws. The court can issue a restraining order to prevent ongoing harm.

2522.plain: This section lets courts and the Attorney General force phone and telecom companies, and their equipment makers and support providers, to follow a federal law requiring their systems to support lawful surveillance. A court may impose a civil (non-criminal) penalty of up to $10,000 per day for not complying with its order.

2523.plain: This section sets the conditions a foreign government must meet before the Attorney General can approve an agreement letting it request electronic data from U.S. communication providers, such as strong privacy protections and a ban on targeting people in the United States or U.S. persons. It also sets up a process for Congress to review and reject such agreements.

2701.plain: It is a federal crime to intentionally get into a computer system that provides electronic communication services (like an email server) without permission, or to go beyond the access allowed. The crime applies when the person then obtains, changes, or blocks authorized access to messages stored in that system.
keyPoints: Access must be intentional and without authorization, or exceed authorization
Must obtain, alter, or block access to stored wire or electronic communications
Does not apply to conduct allowed by the service provider, or by a user for their own messages
Higher penalties if done for profit, malicious damage, or to further another crime or tort
2701.penalty: A fine, up to 1 year in prison, or both for a first offense (up to 5 years for a repeat); if done for profit, malicious damage, or another crime or tort, up to 5 years for a first offense and up to 10 years for a repeat

exceeds an authorization to access that facility
obtains, alters, or prevents authorized access to a wire or electronic communication while it is in electronic storage

act: get into a computer system that provides electronic communication services
go beyond the access allowed
obtains, changes, or blocks authorized access to messages

2702.plain: This section says when companies that provide email, messaging, or online storage to the public may and may not share customers' messages and account records. It bars sharing without a listed reason, such as the customer's consent, a legal order, or an emergency involving risk of death or serious injury, and requires yearly reports to Congress on emergency disclosures.

2703.plain: This section sets the rules for how the government can force online service providers to hand over customers' messages and account records, such as by a warrant (a judge's written permission to search), a subpoena (a legal demand for information), or a court order. It also requires providers to preserve records when asked and lets providers challenge certain demands that would conflict with foreign law.

2704.plain: This section lets the government require an online service provider to make a backup copy of a customer's messages so they are not destroyed while a legal demand is pending. It also explains how the customer can go to court to challenge the demand.

2705.plain: This section lets the government delay telling a customer that it has obtained the customer's online messages or records, for up to 90 days at a time, if telling them could cause harm such as danger to someone, flight, or destroyed evidence. It also lets a court order a provider not to tell anyone about a warrant, subpoena, or court order.

2706.plain: This section requires the government to pay online service providers back for reasonable costs of gathering and providing customer information it requests. Phone toll records and phone listings are generally excluded unless the request was unusually large or burdensome.

2707.plain: This section lets providers, customers, and others harmed by knowing or intentional violations of this chapter sue for money damages (at least $1,000), legal fees, and other relief. It also sets a 2-year deadline to sue, a good-faith defense, and possible discipline for federal employees who violate the chapter.

2708.plain: This section says the remedies and penalties in this chapter are the only court remedies for violations of this chapter that do not involve constitutional rights.

2709.plain: This section requires phone and internet providers to give the FBI certain customer information, such as names, addresses, and billing records, when the FBI certifies it is relevant to an international terrorism or spying investigation. It can bar the provider from telling anyone about the request, subject to court review, and requires reports to Congress.

2710.plain: This section limits when businesses that rent, sell, or deliver videos may share information showing what videos a customer requested or got. Customers whose information is wrongly shared can sue for damages of at least $2,500, and old records must be destroyed.

2712.plain: This section lets people sue the United States for money damages (at least $10,000) when the government willfully violates certain surveillance and stored-communications laws. It sets the procedures and deadlines for these lawsuits.

2713.plain: This section says online service providers must follow this chapter's rules to preserve or hand over customer messages and records even if the data is stored outside the United States.

2721.plain: This section bars State motor vehicle departments and their workers from knowingly sharing personal information from driver and vehicle records, except for listed allowed uses such as government work, safety recalls, court cases, insurance, and uses the person consents to. Stricter rules apply to highly sensitive information. Penalties for violations are set in section 2723.

2722.plain: It is illegal to knowingly get or share personal information from a motor vehicle record for a use the law does not allow. It is also illegal to lie to get personal information from someone's motor vehicle record. This applies to any person.
keyPoints: Obtaining or sharing must be done knowingly
Allowed uses are listed in section 2721(b)
Lying to get someone's motor vehicle record information is also illegal
2722.penalty: No penalty is stated in this section; penalties are set in section 2723
acts: to obtain or disclose personal information, from a motor vehicle record
make false representation to obtain any personal information from an individual's motor vehicle record

act: get or share personal information from a motor vehicle record
lie to get personal information

2723.plain: This section sets the penalties for this chapter: a fine for anyone who knowingly violates it. A State motor vehicle department that regularly fails to follow the chapter can face a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per day.

2724.plain: This section lets a person sue in federal court if someone knowingly gets, shares, or uses their personal information from state motor vehicle (DMV) records for a reason the law does not allow. The court can award money for the harm (at least $2,500), extra punishment money (punitive damages) for willful or reckless violations, lawyer fees, and other relief.
